findings.title: The published image is amd64 only: docker-publish.yml sets up buildx and then never uses it, so ARM self-hosters cannot run VulnRadar at all
findings.description: docker-publish.yml:23 runs `docker/setup-buildx-action`, then lines 49-51 invoke plain `docker build -t ... .` with no `--platform` and no `buildx build`, and lines 53-54 push each tag separately. I fetched the manifest for v3.7.2 from ghcr.io anonymously: it comes back as `application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json`, a single-platform manifest, not an OCI image index or a Docker manifest list. So only the runner's architecture (ubuntu-latest, linux/amd64) is ever built and the buildx setup step has no effect on the build.
findings.impact: Anyone self-hosting on ARM64 (Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, an Ampere or Graviton VPS, which is the cheap tier most hobbyist self-hosters buy) gets `no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8` from `docker compose up -d`, or falls back to qemu emulation with a several-times slowdown on a scanner whose docs promise sub-3-second scans. Nothing in the self-hosting docs states the image is amd64 only.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `docker build`/`docker push` block in docker-publish.yml:45-54 with `docker/build-push-action` using `platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, `push: true`, and `cache-from`/`cache-to: type=gha`. Keep the cosign step signing the resulting index digest. If arm64 build time is unacceptable, say so explicitly in app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx rather than leaving it undocumented.

findings.title: The weekly GHCR cleanup deletes untagged digests with no age gate, so an operator who followed the compose file's own advice to pin by digest loses the ability to pull their image
findings.description: docker-compose.yml:48-51 instructs self-hosters to pin immutably: pull the tag, read the digest with `docker images --digests`, and replace the tag with `ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar@sha256:<digest>`. .github/workflows/ghcr-cleanup.yml:39-45 runs `dataaxiom/ghcr-cleanup-action` every Monday at 06:00 UTC with `delete-untagged: true` and `delete-orphaned-images: true`, and its own header (lines 15-18) states there is deliberately no `older-than` cutoff: "a digest with no tag pointing at it is orphaned the moment it's created". The header also names the exact scenario that untags a live digest (lines 6-8): "any build a tag later moved away from, e.g. a re-run while debugging the release pipeline". Re-running docker-publish.yml for an existing tag produces a new digest (the base image `node:22.11.0-alpine` is a mutable tag and the build is not reproducible), moves `vX.Y.Z` and `latest` onto it, and leaves the previous digest untagged and therefore in scope for deletion at the next scheduled run.
findings.impact: An operator who pinned by digest exactly as the compose file told them to gets `manifest unknown` on the next `docker compose pull`, container restart, or host reboot, and cannot recover the image they were running. There is no dry-run on the scheduled path (line 45 evaluates the expression to `false` for `schedule`), no notification, and no way to restore a deleted GHCR version.
findings.recommendation: Add `older-than: 30 days` to the ghcr-cleanup.yml step so a digest an operator may have pinned in the last month is never removed, or add `keep-n-untagged` so recent orphans survive. Alternatively remove the digest-pinning advice from docker-compose.yml:48-51 and tell operators to pin by version tag only, so the guidance and the retention policy agree.

findings.title: The published scan-gate composite action is documented at the mutable `@main` ref, so every consumer's CI executes whatever is on VulnRadar's unprotected main while holding their VULNRADAR_TOKEN
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:1299 publishes the CI/CD integration snippet as `- uses: ${APP_REPO}/.github/actions/scan-gate@main`, and lib/ai/system-prompt.ts:397 gives the AI assistant the same snippet to hand out, with `api-key: ${{ secrets.VULNRADAR_TOKEN }}` right underneath. .github/actions/scan-gate/action.yml is a composite action whose only step is a `shell: bash` block (lines 76-183), so every consumer runs shell from VulnRadar's default branch at job time. That branch has no protection and no required checks (ci-02) and accepts unreviewed auto-merged dependency bumps (ci-03). Meanwhile every third-party action in this repo's own workflows is pinned by commit SHA (verified: all 23 `uses:` lines carry a 40-hex SHA), so the project applies to itself the standard it does not publish to its users. There is also no ref a consumer could safely pin to instead: all 65 tags are `vX.Y.Z` application releases whose content moves under the action, and no workflow in this repo ever calls the action, so it is entirely untested.
findings.impact: A single push to VulnRadar's main runs immediately in every downstream consumer's CI job, with that job's full secret set and write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN, not merely their VulnRadar API key. For a security vendor shipping a supply-chain-relevant action this is the exact misconfiguration the product is sold to detect. The action being untested also means a change to POST /api/v3/scan's response shape breaks every consumer's pipeline with no signal here.
findings.recommendation: Cut a dedicated moving major tag for the action (`v1`) that only advances after review, update app/docs/api/page.tsx:1299 and lib/ai/system-prompt.ts:397 to `scan-gate@v1` with a note that a SHA pin is stronger, and add a job to ci.yml that runs the action against a known target so its contract is exercised. Fixing ci-02 is a prerequisite for `@main` or `@v1` being trustworthy at all.

findings.title: There is no deploy pipeline, no migration step ordered ahead of new code, and no rollback procedure documented anywhere
findings.description: No workflow in .github/workflows/ deploys anything: ci.yml validates, docker-publish.yml pushes an image on a tag, release.yml attaches artifacts, and the remaining three are housekeeping. The documented upgrade for a self-hoster is app/docs/setup/page.tsx:684, `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`, with no migration step at all. Schema changes are applied by instrumentation.ts at process boot, which is after the new image is already the running container and is serving traffic, so there is no point at which the schema is advanced while the old code is still live. `npm run db:migrate` is mentioned once at app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:547 and again inside an error remediation string at line 570, and per AUDIT-014#host-02 the migrate script is not even present in the published image. Grepping app/docs/, README.md and SECURITY.md for `rollback`, `roll back`, `revert` and `previous version` returns nothing: there is no documented way back. AUDIT-013#migrate-01 established the versioned upgrade path is already missing 11 tables and 8 columns relative to what instrumentation.ts creates, and AUDIT-013#migrate-04 that `db:restore` pipes into psql without `ON_ERROR_STOP`, so the recovery tooling is itself unreliable.
findings.impact: An operator whose upgrade fails at boot (which per AUDIT-014#host-01 is the default on a fresh database) has a crash-looping container, a database that may have been partially altered by the new image's boot DDL, no migrate script inside the image to inspect or re-run, and no documented rollback. Reverting the compose tag is not obviously safe because the old code may not tolerate whatever schema the new boot already applied, and nothing tells the operator that.
findings.recommendation: Add an Upgrading section to app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx that (1) tells the operator to run `npm run db:backup` before pulling, (2) documents `db:migrate` as a distinct step run before the new container takes traffic, and (3) states plainly which schema changes are backward compatible and how to pin back to the previous version tag. Ship scripts/ in the image (AUDIT-014#host-02) so the documented commands are runnable, and state the supported downgrade window.

findings.title: docker-compose.yml mounts no persistent volume for backups or uploads, and /app is root-owned while the process runs as uid 1001, so the app cannot even create the directories its own docs promise
findings.description: Static analysis. The production compose declares one volume, postgres_data (:114-116), and the app service (:52-112) mounts none. Two directories the app writes to are therefore on the container's throwaway writable layer: BACKUP_DIR, which defaults to join(process.cwd(), "backups") in both app/api/v3/admin/backup/route.ts:27 and scripts/backup-db.mjs:184, and the legacy avatar directory join(process.cwd(), "data", "avatars") in lib/uploads/avatar-migration.ts:48. Neither exists in the image, and neither can be created at runtime: the runner stage sets WORKDIR /app as root (Dockerfile:68) before switching to USER nextjs (:102), and the COPY --chown flags at :76-79 only chown the copied children, so /app itself stays root:root and a uid-1001 process cannot mkdir inside it. scripts/backup-db.mjs:200 calls mkdir(backupDir, { recursive: true }) and would fail with EACCES. .env.example:49-51 explicitly warns "On a container this MUST be a persistent/mounted volume, otherwise every backup is lost on the next rebuild/redeploy", and app/docs/setup/page.tsx:684 documents `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d` as the update command, which recreates the container. docker-compose.dev.yml:62-66 does mount avatar_data_dev and its comment says "See docker-compose.yml's avatar_data volume comment", a comment and volume that do not exist in docker-compose.yml.
findings.impact: Backups taken from the admin panel or by cron inside the container land nowhere durable, and would fail on the permission error before that. An operator who follows the .env.example advice has no volume to point BACKUP_DIR at, and BACKUP_DIR is not forwarded to the container anyway (host-03). The dev compose's cross-reference tells the next maintainer a comment exists that does not.
findings.recommendation: Add `backup_data:/app/backups` and `avatar_data:/app/data/avatars` volumes to the app service in docker-compose.yml with matching top-level volume entries, and add `RUN mkdir -p /app/backups /app/data/avatars && chown -R nextjs:nodejs /app/backups /app/data` to the Dockerfile runner stage before USER nextjs at :102. Fix the dangling cross-reference in docker-compose.dev.yml:63.

findings.title: The self-updater advertises itself as supported inside Docker but writes into a root-owned /app as uid 1001, runs a migrate script the image does not contain, and any success is discarded by the documented update command
findings.description: Static trace. isUpdaterSupported() (lib/updater/environment.ts:8-17) returns unsupported only when process.env.VERCEL is set; there is no container detection, so both app/api/v3/admin/updater/status/route.ts:37 and .../apply/route.ts:56 report the updater available inside the official image and the admin UI offers it. runUpdateJob then sets appRoot = process.cwd() (lib/updater/apply.ts:206), which is /app, and calls copyTreeOverlay(sourceRoot, appRoot) at :261 to write the release's full source tree there. /app is root:root because WORKDIR /app runs as root at Dockerfile:68 and the process runs as USER nextjs (uid 1001) from :102, so creating new top-level entries such as /app/lib or /app/app fails with EACCES, while pre-existing chowned files such as /app/package.json and /app/next.config.mjs would be overwritten in place first (overwriting an existing file needs write on the file, not the directory). The job then fails with a raw permission error after package.json has already been replaced with the new release's copy while node_modules and .next are still the old build. Even if the copy succeeded, the npm-ci step at :325 and the `npm run db:migrate -- --yes` step at :353 run against a tree with no scripts/ (host-02), and the final log line at :369 asks the admin to run `npm run build` and restart, which in a container means the next `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d` (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:684) throws the whole writable layer away. AUDIT-013#cov-06 recorded that this pipeline has 0% test coverage and AUDIT-013#migrate-01 that the migrate step it invokes stamps 3.0.0 on a schema missing 11 tables; this finding is about the updater being reachable at all in the deployment shape where it cannot work.
findings.impact: A self-hosting admin sees an in-app Update button, clicks it, and gets a half-applied file copy plus an opaque EACCES in the job log, with package.json now describing a version whose code is not installed. In the worst case they then follow the log's advice and restart, and the update silently disappears on the next image pull.
findings.recommendation: Extend isUpdaterSupported() in lib/updater/environment.ts to detect a container (existence of /.dockerenv, or an explicit CONTAINER/VULNRADAR_UPDATER_DISABLED env var set in the Dockerfile) and return supported: false with a reason pointing at `docker compose pull`. If in-container updating is wanted instead, chown /app to nextjs:nodejs in the runner stage and ship scripts/ (host-02).

findings.title: API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is defaulted to an empty string in compose instead of being a required substitution, so a missing key produces a crash-looping container rather than a compose-time error naming the variable
findings.description: Static analysis. lib/config/env.ts:19-26 requires API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY to be exactly 64 characters, and instrumentation.ts:33-35 calls validateEnv() as the first thing register() does, so an empty value throws before anything else. docker-compose.yml:61 passes it as `${API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-}`, which substitutes the empty string when the variable is absent from .env. Compare docker-compose.yml:23, where POSTGRES_PASSWORD uses `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}` and compose refuses to start with a named error. The result of the inconsistency is that the one variable .env.example:27 ships blank by design (API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY= with no value) is also the one that fails latest and least legibly: `docker compose up -d` reports success, and the operator has to run `docker compose logs app` on a restart-looping container to find the zod message. The Dockerfile comment at :41-44 explains the deliberate decision not to set a build-time placeholder so operators must inject a real key, which is right, but the compose file then undoes the loud failure that decision was meant to produce.
findings.impact: The single most commonly missed self-host variable produces a container that reports as started and then crash-loops, indistinguishable at the `docker compose ps` level from the empty-database crash-loop in host-01. The operator has to correlate two different failures from the same symptom.
findings.recommendation: Change docker-compose.yml:61 and docker-compose.dev.yml:51 to `${API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY:?Set API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY in .env (64 hex chars: node -e \"console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))\")}` so the failure happens at compose parse time with the generation command in the message.

findings.title: Every API-key response example in the docs uses field names and a status the routes do not return (`prefix` vs `key_prefix`, a top-level `id`/`name` that does not exist, 200 vs 201)
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:727-735 documents POST /keys as returning `{ id, name, key: { raw_key, prefix, daily_limit } }`. app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:120 returns `ApiResponse.success({ key }, 201)`, and lib/api/api-utils.ts:15 emits the payload verbatim, so the real body is `{ "key": { id, key_prefix, name, daily_limit, created_at, scopes, raw_key } }` with status 201: there is no top-level `id` or `name`, and the field is `key_prefix` (lib/api/api-keys.ts:92/107), not `prefix`. GET /keys (app/docs/api/page.tsx:702-714) has the same problem: lib/api/api-keys.ts:617 selects `ak.key_prefix`, and also returns `scopes` and `usage_today`, neither of which the example shows. POST /keys/{id}/rotate (:763-767) documents `{ id, name, key: { raw_key, prefix, daily_limit } }`; app/api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate/route.ts:62-72 returns `{ success: true, key: { id, key_prefix, name, daily_limit, created_at, raw_key, scopes } }`. The docs also omit the 403 "API keys are disabled on this deployment" (app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:38) and the 400 "Invalid key ID" on rotate/revoke.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the three response examples in app/docs/api/page.tsx:702-795 from the actual RETURNING clauses in lib/api/api-keys.ts:92 and :617, mark POST /keys as 201, add `scopes` and `usage_today` to the GET example, and add the missing 400/403 rows to each error list.
findings.impact: A client written against the documented shape reads `response.id` and `response.key.prefix` and gets undefined for both, and a client that asserts on HTTP 200 rejects the successful 201 from key creation. This is the first call any integration makes.

findings.title: Key rotation is documented as a hard-delete-and-recreate in three places; the route updates the same row in place and keeps the id
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:754 describes POST /keys/{id}/rotate as "Hard-delete the key and create a new one with the same name" and its example (:763-767) shows a new id (2) replacing id 1; :1146-1147 repeats "rotate with POST /api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate, which deletes the old key in the same call"; lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:438-439 says "Delete the key and issue a replacement". lib/api/api-keys.ts:637-700 does the opposite and says so explicitly: "Rotate an API key - swaps the secret in place, same row, same id", with the comment at :664-671 explaining that the old delete-then-insert wiped api_usage rows via ON DELETE CASCADE and was deliberately replaced by `UPDATE api_keys SET key_hash = ..., key_prefix = ... WHERE id = $7 AND user_id = $8`.
findings.impact: An operator who stores key ids (audit records, per-key dashboards, allow-lists) is told rotation invalidates the id and rebuilds their mapping after every rotation, which it does not. The reverse is also missed: because the id and its usage history survive, today's consumed quota carries over to the rotated key, which the docs never mention.
findings.recommendation: Change app/docs/api/page.tsx:754 and :1146-1147 and lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:438-439 to "replaces the key's secret in place; the id, name, scopes and today's usage count are preserved", and update the response example at :763-767 to keep the original id.

findings.title: New API keys are documented as getting a daily limit of 50 from CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT; the route always passes the plan's apiRequestsPerDay instead
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:738 states "Default daily_limit comes from CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT (50)" and its example (:733) shows `"daily_limit": 50`; app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:172-174 repeats "New API keys default to CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT = 50". app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:88-97 resolves `dailyLimit = planLimits ? planLimits.apiRequestsPerDay : -1` and calls `generateApiKey(userId, name, dailyLimit === -1 ? 999999 : dailyLimit, scopes)`, always supplying a concrete value, so lib/api/api-keys.ts:70's `dailyLimit ?? getSetting("DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT")` fallback is never reached from this route. lib/billing/catalog.ts gives apiRequestsPerDay 25 (free, :118), 100 (core, :150), 5000 (pro, :182) and -1 (elite, :213, stored as 999999). app/api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate/route.ts:41-42 does the same.
findings.impact: A free-tier user is told their new key allows 50 requests/day and is cut off at 25; a Pro user is told 50 and actually has 5,000. Both numbers on the two doc pages are wrong for every plan, and the named constant is dead on this path.
findings.recommendation: Replace app/docs/api/page.tsx:738 and app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:172-174 with "a new key's daily_limit is your plan's apiRequestsPerDay (lib/billing/catalog.ts): 25 / 100 / 5,000 / effectively unlimited", and either delete CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT or document that it applies only to keys created outside this route.

findings.title: DELETE /history documents a `{ success: true, deleted: 47 }` response that the route never returns, and claims it deletes every scan when it excludes GitHub repo scans
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:461-468 describes DELETE /history as "Permanently delete every scan and tag for the authenticated user" with the response `{ "success": true, "deleted": 47 }`. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:226 returns `ApiResponse.success({ message: SUCCESS_MESSAGES.DELETED })`, and lib/api/api-utils.ts:15 passes the object through unchanged, so the real body is `{ "message": "..." }` with no `success` key and no count. The DELETE statements at :215-224 are scoped with `AND (scan_type IS NULL OR scan_type != 'github')`, so GitHub repo scans survive. The error list (:468) shows only 401; the route also returns 403 for an unaccepted ToS (:169) and for a key missing scan:delete (:176-180), and 429 for the key's daily limit (:186-191).
findings.impact: A client that branches on `response.success` treats every successful wipe as a failure, and one that reports "deleted N scans" prints undefined. An integrator with repo scans is told they were deleted when they were not. The scan:delete scope requirement is invisible here even though it is deliberately excluded from a new key's default scopes (lib/config/client-constants.ts:335-338), so this call 403s for most keys with no documented reason.
findings.recommendation: Correct the response example in app/docs/api/page.tsx:464-467 to the real `{ message }` body (or make the route return `{ success: true, deleted: n }` from a RETURNING count), state that GitHub repo scans are excluded, and add the 403 (scan:delete missing) and 429 rows to the error list.

findings.title: GET /history is documented as showing teammates' scans; the query is scoped to the caller's own user_id with no team clause
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:424 notes "Team members can see scans from other team members in the same team" on the GET /history card. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:117-138 issues `SELECT ... FROM scan_history sh WHERE sh.user_id = $1 AND (sh.scan_type IS NULL OR sh.scan_type != 'github') ORDER BY sh.scanned_at DESC LIMIT ...` in both retention branches: there is no team_id join and no union with team_members. Team visibility exists only on GET /history/{id} (app/api/v3/history/[id]/route.ts:15-18, getTeamResourceAccess) and on the separate GET /api/v3/teams/member-scans route, which app/docs/teams/page.tsx:409 documents correctly.
findings.impact: A team lead is told the list endpoint aggregates the team and sees only their own scans, with no error to explain the gap, and never finds /teams/member-scans, which the API reference does not mention at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete the note at app/docs/api/page.tsx:424 or replace it with "this list is your own scans only; use GET /api/v3/teams/member-scans?teamId=&userId= for a teammate's scans, and GET /history/{id} for a single scan a teammate owns".

findings.title: GET /history documents its `id` field as a number; the route returns the opaque public_id string
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:409-421 shows the GET /history response with `"id": 1`, and the code samples at :946 and :981 and the Python sample at :1011 all use the numeric form `/history/123`. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:117 and :127 both select `sh.public_id AS id`, so the returned id is the opaque non-enumerable token, not the row's integer primary key. GET /history/{id} resolves either form (lib/history/resolve-scan.ts:56-67 matches public_id first and falls back to the legacy numeric id), so the samples still work, but the documented list-response type does not match what comes back.
findings.impact: A client that declares `id: number` (or does `Number(scan.id)`) against the documented shape gets NaN for every row and cannot build a detail URL. The docs also never mention that the opaque id is the canonical form and the numeric one is legacy.
findings.recommendation: Change the example at app/docs/api/page.tsx:412 to a string public id, add a note that `id` is an opaque token and that /history/{id} also accepts the legacy numeric id, and mirror the same wording on the GET /history/{id} card at :430-456.

findings.title: History retention is documented as Free 30 days / Core 90 days; every plan's shipped retention default is -1 (keep forever)
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:408 states "Retention follows the user's plan (Free: 30 days, Core: 90, Pro/Elite: forever)". app/api/v3/history/route.ts:26-32 resolves retention through the registry keys BILLING_FREE_RETENTION / BILLING_CORE_SUPPORTER_RETENTION / BILLING_PRO_SUPPORTER_RETENTION / BILLING_ELITE_SUPPORTER_RETENTION, whose shipped defaults are all -1 (lib/config/config-values.ts:1209-1212, with the comment at :1205-1208 "-1 means keep forever on every plan"). :110-114 turns any value <= 0 into the no-retention-window branch, so on a default deployment no scan is ever aged out for any plan.
findings.impact: Free and Core users are told their history is deleted after 30 or 90 days when it is kept indefinitely, which is both a factual error and, since it is a data-retention statement, one the privacy/legal pages have to agree with. A self-hoster reading it also believes a cleanup window is running that is not.
findings.recommendation: Change app/docs/api/page.tsx:408 to say retention is admin-configurable per plan and defaults to unlimited on every plan (lib/config/config-values.ts:1209-1212), and reconcile the free plan's "30-day scan history" marketing bullet in lib/billing/catalog.ts:110 with whichever value is intended.

findings.title: The documented five X-RateLimit-* headers on a successful response are not what the documented endpoints send: session-auth scans send none
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:1376-1386 shows a 200 response carrying X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, -Used, -Policy and -Reset, and :1405-1412 states "Both emit the same X-RateLimit-* headers". app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:280-283 goes further: "Every successful scan response includes rate-limit headers." In app/api/v3/scan/route.ts the success path at :441-452 attaches only Limit, Remaining and Reset, and only on the API-key branch; the session-cookie branch returns `NextResponse.json({ scanId, status })` at :454 with no rate-limit headers at all. The five-header helper getRateLimitHeaders (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:408-423) is the only source of X-RateLimit-Used and X-RateLimit-Policy, and across all of app/api it is called on exactly four lines: scan/route.ts:214, scan/crawl/route.ts:183, scan/bulk/route.ts:575 (all 429 paths) and scan/bulk/route.ts:732 (the one success path that uses it). GET /history, GET /history/{id} and GET /scan/status/{id} send no rate-limit headers on any path.
findings.impact: The docs' own best practice, "Read X-RateLimit-Remaining, not the 429" (app/docs/api/page.tsx:1489), cannot be followed on the endpoint it is written for when the caller uses a session, and X-RateLimit-Used / -Policy never appear on a 200 outside bulk. A client that pre-emptively throttles on those headers silently never throttles.
findings.recommendation: Either call getRateLimitHeaders on the success responses of app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:441-454 (both branches) and the history reads, or scope the claim in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1376-1412 and app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:280-283 to "POST /scan/bulk on the session path, and Limit/Remaining/Reset only on Bearer scan creation".

findings.title: The OpenAPI spec declares Bearer API-key security on five endpoint groups that only accept a session cookie
findings.description: lib/api/openapi-spec.ts declares `security: [{ apiKey: [] }]` on /scan/remediation (:337), /scan/remediation/bulk (:369), /keys GET and POST (:392, :403), /keys/{id}/rotate (:440) and /revoke (:466), /domains (:481, :492, :522), /domains/{id}/verify (:558), /schedules (:578, :589) and /teams (:617, :628), while each description simultaneously says "Session cookie auth.". The routes confirm the session-only gate and never call validateApiKey: app/api/v3/scan/remediation/route.ts:52, app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:23/33, app/api/v3/domains/route.ts:21/55/145, app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts (GET/POST), app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:18/50. Grepping BEARER_PREFIX/validateApiKey across app/api returns exactly 16 route files, none of them these. The apiKey scheme is the document's only securityScheme (:679-686), so there is no cookie scheme to point at instead.
findings.impact: The spec is the machine-readable contract: importing it into Postman/Insomnia/Bruno configures a Bearer token for 14 of the 26 documented operations, all of which then return 401. The playground has the same problem in reverse: it gates "Send request" on an API key being pasted (app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:452) and then succeeds only because the browser happens to attach a same-origin session cookie, so the key it demanded was never used.
findings.recommendation: Add a `cookieAuth` securityScheme (`type: apiKey, in: cookie`) to lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:679-686 and set `security: [{ cookieAuth: [] }]` on the session-only operations, so a spec consumer is told the truth and the playground can label those operations "browser session required".

findings.title: The OpenAPI spec omits ten HTTP methods that exist on paths it already documents
findings.description: Mechanically diffing the 20 path items in lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:56-677 against the exported handlers in the matching route.ts files: /history documents GET but the route also exports DELETE (app/api/v3/history/route.ts:153); /history/{id} documents GET but the route also exports PATCH (:194) and DELETE (:392); /scan/remediation documents POST but the route also exports GET (:147) and DELETE (:116); /schedules documents GET+POST but the route also exports PATCH (:223) and DELETE (:322); /teams documents GET+POST but the route also exports PATCH (:129) and DELETE (:176). Ten real operations, on paths the spec already lists, are missing. app/docs/triage/page.tsx:383-394 and app/docs/teams/page.tsx:447-509 document most of them in prose, so the spec is the outlier, not the routes.
findings.impact: The playground renders only what the spec lists (app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:61-104), so a user can create a schedule or a team from it but cannot rename, pause or delete one, and cannot clear or annotate history. Anyone generating a client SDK from the spec gets a write-only API for those resources.
findings.recommendation: Add the ten missing operations to lib/api/openapi-spec.ts (delete on /history and /history/{id}, patch on /history/{id}, get+delete on /scan/remediation with its ?url= and ?findingId= query params, patch+delete on /schedules and /teams), and extend tests/lib/api/openapi-spec.test.ts with a check that every documented path's method set matches the route file's exports.

findings.title: The webhooks doc says the free plan gets 0 webhooks in four places; lib/billing/catalog.ts gives it 1
findings.description: app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx states the free-plan webhook cap as 0 four separate times: the hero stat "0-∞" (:58), the overview paragraph (:75-79), the POST /webhooks note (:181), and the Security section bullet (:422). lib/billing/catalog.ts:121 sets `webhooks: 1` for the free plan (its own feature bullet at :112 reads "1 webhook alert"), and core_supporter is also 1 (:153), pro 5 (:185), elite -1 (:216). app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:100-107 enforces exactly that value via withinPlanLimit(count, planLimits.webhooks).
findings.impact: Free users, the largest cohort, are told a feature they have is unavailable and never set up the webhook they are entitled to. The Core tier's cap is also mislabeled: 0 to 1 is presented as the paid upgrade when the real step up is 1 to 5 at Pro.
findings.recommendation: Change all four occurrences in app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx (:58, :75-79, :181, :422) to "1 on Free, 1 on Core Supporter, 5 on Pro Supporter, unlimited on Elite Supporter", and derive them from lib/billing/catalog.ts rather than hardcoding, so the next plan change cannot desync them again.

findings.title: PATCH /webhooks (test) is documented as returning your endpoint's status code, and the test delivery is sent unsigned and without the documented User-Agent
findings.description: app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:200 describes the test endpoint as "Returns the response status from your endpoint" and :204-207 shows `{ "success": true, "status": 204 }`. app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:293-296 returns `{ success: true, message: "Test webhook sent successfully" }`: there is no `status` field on any path. Separately, :277-281 sends the test payload with only `{ "Content-Type": "application/json" }`, while a real delivery (lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:74-78) adds `User-Agent: VulnRadar-Webhook/1.0` and `X-VulnRadar-Signature: sha256=<hmac>`. The docs state the opposite at :369 ("Delivered with ... User-Agent: VulnRadar-Webhook/1.0") and :397-405 ("Every delivery includes X-VulnRadar-Signature").
findings.impact: A consumer that follows the Security section and rejects unsigned payloads fails the Test button, which is the documented way to confirm the webhook works (:449-453), and gets a non-2xx back that the app reports as a broken webhook. Any client reading `status` off the test response gets undefined.
findings.recommendation: Fix the example at app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:204-207 to `{ success: true, message: "..." }` and the description at :200, and make app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:277-281 build its headers through the same helper lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:74-78 uses so a test is signed exactly like a real delivery.

findings.title: The compiled AI knowledge truncates 20 of 52 docs callouts mid-sentence at 300 characters and leaks 64 raw JSX `{" "}` tokens and 19 undecoded HTML entities
findings.description: scripts/compile-docs-knowledge.mjs:274 and :284 both apply `stripJsx(...).slice(0, 300)` to every DocsCallout body. Measured across app/docs/*/page.tsx, 52 callouts are extracted and 20 exceed 300 stripped characters, so they land in lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md cut mid-word: for example the API page's Scopes callout ends at "returns 403 naming" (docs-knowledge.md:997) and the CI/CD callout ends at "before ch" (:1009). The offending pages are app/docs/api (2), config (2), github (2), rate-limits (2), scheduled-scans (2), self-hosting (4), sharing (2), account-security, developers, teams and triage. stripJsx (:82-110) also never strips the JSX whitespace literal `{" "}` (64 occurrences survive into the output) and never decodes `'`, `{` or `}` (19 occurrences), so those consume part of the same 300-char budget.
findings.impact: lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md is what the in-product AI assistant answers from. Twenty of the most important "be careful about this" notes reach it as unfinished sentences, so the assistant either invents the missing half or drops the caveat. The Scopes callout in particular loses the sentence that tells the user a 403 names the missing scope.
findings.recommendation: Raise the cap in scripts/compile-docs-knowledge.mjs:274/284 to at least 1200 characters (the longest real callout is 522), or truncate on a sentence boundary; and add `.replace(/\{\s*"\s*"\s*\}/g, " ")` plus `'`/`&#\d+;` decoding to stripJsx before the existing entity replacements.

findings.title: The API error-code table documents 422 for SSRF and private-IP rejections that actually return 400, and omits 402, 409, 413, 502 and 503
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:1458-1463 defines 422 as "The target is unreachable, blocks the request, resolves to a private IP, or fails the SSRF check", and the best-practice at :1494-1496 tells the reader a client-side check "turns a 422 round trip into a local error". app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:276-282 returns 400 for a failed validateScanTarget, :265-273 returns 400 for an invalid URL, and :285-296 returns 403 for a blocked target: POST /scan never returns 422. Grepping every route.ts for `status: 422` finds four files only: scan/authenticated (login failure, :344/:347), demo-scan (:175), and history/[id]/ports (:96). The table also omits five codes the documented surface really returns: 402 (Browserbase minute quota, app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:92), 409 (already-terminal scan cancel, app/api/v3/scan/status/[id]/route.ts, and documented on that endpoint card at :127 but absent from the table), 413 (app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts:143), 502 (app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:392) and 503 (11 route files).
findings.impact: A generic error handler written from this table treats an SSRF rejection as a retryable 422 and never handles the 400 it actually gets, and has no branch for the 402/409/413/502/503 responses the API really produces.
findings.recommendation: Correct the 422 row in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1458-1463 to "login could not be confirmed on POST /scan/authenticated, or a target that could not be reached on the demo and port endpoints", move SSRF and private-IP rejection to the 400 row, fix the best-practice sentence at :1494-1496, and add rows for 402, 409, 413, 502 and 503.

findings.title: CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-PR checklist covers two of the seven CI gates and never mentions that the repository has tests
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md:55 says 'Ensure npm run build and npm run lint pass locally', and its script table at :17-24 lists dev, build, lint, lint:fix, typecheck and format. .github/workflows/ci.yml gates a PR on seven things: npm run lint (:40), npm run format:check (:44), npx tsc --noEmit (:67), npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev (:71), a regenerate-and-diff of the AI knowledge files (:73-82, which runs npm run build:knowledge and then `git diff --exit-code -- lib/ai lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts`), npm run test (:107), node --test in cli/ (:112), plus the extension's own typecheck, format:check and both builds (:141-149) and finally npm run build (:196). CONTRIBUTING never mentions tests, formatting checks, the extension jobs, or the knowledge regeneration, and the repo's own AGENTS.md 'Before every commit' list (:173-205) also omits format:check, the CLI test, the extension gates and the knowledge diff.
findings.impact: The knowledge-file gate is the trap: any PR that edits a docs page, the changelog data, a check definition or a legal page fails CI with a `git diff --exit-code` error unless the contributor ran npm run build:knowledge and committed the regenerated lib/ai/*.md. Nothing in CONTRIBUTING or AGENTS tells them that. A contributor who follows CONTRIBUTING exactly still gets a red build, on the one step that is least self-explanatory.
findings.recommendation: Replace CONTRIBUTING.md:55 with the full local equivalent of CI: `npm run lint && npm run format:check && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build`, plus `npm run build:knowledge` and commit the result whenever docs, changelog, checks or legal pages change, plus `cd cli && node --test` and `cd extension && npm run typecheck && npm run format:check` when those directories change. Add the same four missing steps to AGENTS.md:173-205 so both the human and the agent checklist match ci.yml.

findings.title: AGENTS.md lists 12 of the scanner's 18 categories, so an automated contributor is told six live categories do not exist
findings.description: AGENTS.md:140-153 gives the authoritative category list an agent must consult 'Before adding a scanner' and names 12: headers, ssl, tls, content, cookies, configuration, information-disclosure, dns, email, api, code, secrets-extended. The Category union at lib/scanner/types.ts:22-39 has 18, adding vibe-code, client-side, supply-chain, host-validation, reputation and active-probes. lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts:7 records EXACT_CHECK_CATEGORY_COUNT = 18, README.md:12 and :30 say 18, and the browser extension's own list at extension/src/lib/categories.ts has all 18. AGENTS.md is the only surface that disagrees, and it has a matching lib/scanner/checks-data/<category>.json for each of the six it omits.
findings.impact: An automated contributor following AGENTS.md sees no vibe-code, client-side, supply-chain, host-validation, reputation or active-probes category and will either refuse to place a check there or invent a new category rather than using the existing one. active-probes matters most: it is the only opt-in, writes-to-the-target category (lib/scanner/types.ts:41-50 explains why it is excluded from ALL_CATEGORIES) and an agent that does not know it exists cannot honour that contract.
findings.recommendation: Replace the hand-written list in AGENTS.md:140-153 with the 18 names from lib/scanner/types.ts, or better, replace it with an instruction to read the Category union directly so it cannot drift again. Add a line stating that active-probes never runs by default and must be named explicitly.

findings.title: The docs nav bills /docs/config as 'Every CONFIG_* value and every environment variable'; the page names 76 of 308 constants and 206 of 267 runtime settings are never named anywhere
findings.description: components/docs/docs-nav.ts:82-85 gives /docs/config the summary 'Every CONFIG_* value and every environment variable'. lib/config/config-values.ts defines 308 `export const CONFIG_*` constants; app/docs/config/page.tsx names 76 of them. lib/config/registry.ts defines 267 SETTINGS_REGISTRY entries, and lib/config/runtime-config.ts:81-94 resolves each one as `database value ?? process.env[key] ?? shipped default`, which means every one of those 267 keys is a valid environment variable name. Only 61 of the 267 appear anywhere on the config page, and almost all of those appear only in their CONFIG_-prefixed form, so the page never tells the reader that the bare key is the environment variable. app/docs/config/page.tsx:605-627 does document the resolution order correctly but never lists which keys participate.
findings.impact: A self-hoster who wants to pin a rate limit, a scan timeout or a billing limit through the environment (the documented way for a container to override without a database write) has no way to learn the variable name short of reading lib/config/registry.ts. The nav summary promises completeness the page does not deliver, so the reader stops looking after not finding their value.
findings.recommendation: Generate the reference rather than hand-writing it: emit a table from SETTINGS_REGISTRY (key, tier, type, default, group, help, all of which the registry already carries) at build time the way scripts/compile-checks-knowledge.mjs already generates check-stats, and render it on /docs/config. Until then, change the nav summary at components/docs/docs-nav.ts:84 to something honest such as 'How configuration resolves, and the values you are most likely to change'.

findings.title: README describes two configuration layers and says the static layer requires an edit and a rebuild; there are three layers and 239 of 268 settings are runtime-editable with no rebuild
findings.description: README.md:88-102 states VulnRadar has 'two configuration layers', describes lib/config/config-values.ts as 'Static app config ... App name, URL, emails, SEO metadata, rate limits, feature flags, billing plans. Edit and rebuild', and closes with 'Self-hosters edit config-values.ts and nothing else'. .env.example:329-330 repeats it: 'These values are NOT in .env. Edit lib/config/config-values.ts directly and rebuild'. In reality lib/config/registry.ts carries 267 SETTINGS_REGISTRY entries of which 239 are `tier: "runtime"` and 29 are `tier: "build"`, lib/config/runtime-config.ts:81-94 resolves each as database ?? env ?? default with a 30 second cache, and components/admin/features/system-settings-manager.tsx renders the whole registry as an editable admin Settings page. Rate limits, feature flags, billing limits, scan timeouts and AI budgets, the very examples the README puts in the 'edit and rebuild' row, are all runtime tier. app/docs/config/page.tsx:580-627 documents this correctly, so the README and .env.example contradict the docs page they link to.
findings.impact: A self-hoster rebuilds and redeploys an image to change a rate limit or a feature flag that they could have changed in the admin panel in five seconds, or sets an environment variable and concludes it does not work because the README told them the value is compiled in. The database layer, which is the one the admin panel writes and the one that wins, is not mentioned in the README at all.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite README.md:88-106 as three layers: database (admin Settings, wins, no restart), environment (a variable named exactly like the SETTINGS_REGISTRY key), and the shipped CONFIG_* default in config-values.ts (edit and rebuild, and required only for the 29 build-tier values). Delete 'Self-hosters edit config-values.ts and nothing else' at :102 and fix the same claim at .env.example:329-330.

findings.title: The crawl page caps are documented as 15 and 20 in six places; the real caps are per-plan 25 to 250 and 500 for discovery, and the MAX_PAGES constant the docs cite no longer exists
findings.description: The real caps: lib/billing/crawl-page-limits.ts:19-24 sets CRAWL_PAGE_SELECTION_LIMITS to free 25, core_supporter 50, pro_supporter 100, elite_supporter 250, and app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts:257-268 enforces it, treating a billing-disabled (self-hosted) caller as unlimited. Discovery is capped by CONFIG_CRAWL_DISCOVER_MAX_PAGES = 500 (lib/config/config-values.ts:594), read at app/api/v3/scan/crawl/discover/route.ts:74-79. Neither route defines a MAX_PAGES symbol any more. Six surfaces still say 15 or 20: cli/README.md:34 and cli/lib.mjs:126 ('Crawl and scan up to 15 pages'), app/docs/cli/page.tsx:135, app/docs/developers/page.tsx:64, lib/ai/system-prompt.ts:210 ('Crawl + scan up to 15 pages'), and lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:96. The API reference repeats it at app/docs/api/page.tsx:322, :332 ('Max 15 pages (MAX_PAGES in app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts)') and :364 ('Returns up to 20 URLs (MAX_PAGES in app/api/v3/scan/crawl/discover/route.ts)'); those three belong to the API-reference agent's surface and are noted here only so the fix is done in one pass. lib/changelog/data.ts:793 already records the change to 500 discovered and per-plan selection, so the docs are behind their own changelog.
findings.impact: Paying users are told their crawl covers 15 pages when an elite plan covers 250, so they under-use what they paid for and may buy a competitor for site-wide coverage. Self-hosters, who are uncapped, are told they are capped at 15. The AI assistant repeats the wrong number because lib/ai/system-prompt.ts:210 carries it. Two doc lines also cite a constant name that a reader will grep for and not find.
findings.recommendation: Import the numbers instead of writing them. On app/docs/cli/page.tsx and app/docs/developers/page.tsx render CRAWL_PAGE_SELECTION_LIMITS from lib/billing/crawl-page-limits.ts and CONFIG_CRAWL_DISCOVER_MAX_PAGES, the same way app/docs/developers/page.tsx:117 already renders ALL_CATEGORIES. Reword cli/README.md:34 and cli/lib.mjs:126 to 'Crawl and scan the pages your plan allows (self-hosted: unlimited)'. Update lib/ai/system-prompt.ts:210 and recompile the knowledge files.

findings.title: SECURITY.md points reporters at a PGP key and an Acknowledgments list that security.txt does not contain, and scopes out deployments that ignore a hardening guide that does not exist
findings.description: public/.well-known/security.txt has exactly six fields: Contact, Expires (2028-06-18, in the future, correct), Preferred-Languages, Canonical, Policy and Acknowledgments (pointing at https://vulnradar.dev/changelog). SECURITY.md:16 says to email security@vulnradar.dev '(PGP key below)'; SECURITY.md:64-68 then says 'We accept reports encrypted to the PGP key published in public/.well-known/security.txt'. There is no Encryption: field and no key in that file, so a reporter who wants to encrypt has nothing to encrypt to and is told to ask for the fingerprint by unencrypted email. SECURITY.md:26 offers credit 'in the Acknowledgments section of public/.well-known/security.txt' and :62 says 'See public/.well-known/security.txt for the latest list'; the file has no list, only a URL to the changelog. Separately, SECURITY.md:57 puts 'Self-hosted deployments that don't follow our hardening guide' out of scope, and no self-hosting hardening guide exists: grepping for 'harden' across app/docs/ and the root markdown returns only SECURITY-POSTURE.md, which is a checklist for vulnradar.dev's own Cloudflare and ProtonMail records and is not linked from SECURITY.md, README.md or any docs page.
findings.impact: A researcher who follows the published policy cannot encrypt a report, cannot see who has been credited, and is told their self-host finding may be rejected against a document they cannot read. The address itself is real and consistent (CONFIG_SECURITY_EMAIL at lib/config/config-values.ts:155), so the process fails only on the parts SECURITY.md invented.
findings.recommendation: Either publish a key and add `Encryption: https://vulnradar.dev/.well-known/pgp-key.txt` to security.txt, or delete the PGP claims at SECURITY.md:16 and :64-68. Point the Acknowledgments claims at whatever page actually lists credited researchers, or drop them. Either write a self-hosting hardening guide and link it from SECURITY.md:57, or narrow that exclusion to something checkable such as 'deployments running with DISABLE_CSP=1 or without TLS'.

findings.title: The architecture doc's permissions section cites a deleted lib/auth/permissions.ts, three symbols that do not exist, and a role ladder missing 5 of the 9 real roles with every level number wrong
findings.description: app/docs/architecture/page.tsx:540-556 documents the role hierarchy as `user (0) -> support (1) -> moderator (2) -> admin (3)` and lists 'lib/auth/permissions.ts: server-safe role + permission maps (ROLES, ROLE_PERMISSIONS, userHasPermission, canManageRole)'. lib/auth/permissions.ts was removed by commit 4b8d6e71 ('fix: remove dead legacy permission system, fix stale role-name lists'); the file is gone and ROLES, ROLE_PERMISSIONS and userHasPermission do not appear anywhere in lib/. The real model is lib/config/client-constants.ts:12-49, which defines nine roles (user, support, billing, security_analyst, content_manager, ops, moderator, admin, super_admin) with STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY levels 0, 10, 20, 20, 20, 20, 30, 40, 50, plus lib/auth/permissions-client.ts (STAFF_PERMISSIONS, hasStaffPermission, canManageRole, getRoleLevel, hasGodMode) and lib/auth/authorization.ts (requireStaff, requireModerator, requireAdmin, requirePermission). The doc omits the four lateral specialist roles and super_admin, and all four level numbers it does give are wrong.
findings.impact: A contributor reading the architecture doc to understand authorization opens a path that does not exist, greps for three symbols that do not exist, and comes away believing there are four roles when there are nine. Missing super_admin from the doc is the material part: it is the god-mode tier, it is auto-assigned to the first account, and app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:642-647 refuses to assign it through any UI, so anyone reasoning about admin security from this page reasons about the wrong model.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite app/docs/architecture/page.tsx:540-556 against lib/config/client-constants.ts:12-49: render STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY rather than hand-typing it, note that the four level-20 roles are lateral specialists rather than a rung, and note that super_admin is bootstrap-only and un-assignable. Point the file list at lib/auth/permissions-client.ts and lib/auth/authorization.ts.

findings.title: Two 'every script' inventories list 15 and 9 of the 35 npm scripts, omitting every database diagnostic, repair, backup and restore command the repo ships
findings.description: app/docs/developers/page.tsx:504 says 'Every npm script and what it does. Defined in package.json' and then tables 15 of the 35 scripts in package.json. scripts/README.md:49 heads a table 'Available scripts' with 9. Between them they never mention db:diagnose, db:diagnose-2fa, db:repair, db:repair-2fa, db:repair-sequences, db:migrate-avatars, db:backup, db:restore, docs:compile, changelog:compile, checks:compile, legal:compile or build:knowledge. scripts/README.md's directory tree at :10-46 is separately stale: it lists 9 of the 25 files in scripts/_lib/, omits all 12 root-level scripts (backup-db.mjs, restore-db.mjs, build-og-image.mjs, the four compile-*-knowledge.mjs, db-diagnose.mjs, db-diagnose-2fa.mjs, db-repair.mjs, db-repair-2fa.mjs, db-repair-sequences.mjs, migrate-avatars-to-files.mjs) and omits create-fresh-db/schemas/instrumentation-v2.ts. This extends AUDIT-013#dead-04 (which found the archived migrator entry in the same tree) and AUDIT-013#dead-10 (which found the find-duplicate-ids.mjs 'CI gate' claim at :20 and :63 that no workflow runs).
findings.impact: An operator whose database is in a bad state has five purpose-built diagnostic and repair tools in the repo and no document that mentions any of them. That is the direct cause of the impossible recovery advice in doc-05 and it compounds AUDIT-013#migrate-15, which found that nothing documents what to do when a migration fails. db:backup and db:restore are undocumented in these two inventories even though app/docs/config/page.tsx:999-1002 refers to them as if they were.
findings.recommendation: Generate both tables from package.json rather than maintaining them by hand, or at minimum add the 20 missing entries to app/docs/developers/page.tsx:504 and the 8 missing db:* commands to scripts/README.md:49. Regenerate the scripts/README.md tree from an actual listing of scripts/. Add a short 'when something is wrong with the database' section that names db:diagnose, db:diagnose-2fa, db:repair, db:repair-2fa and db:repair-sequences with their dry-run defaults.

findings.title: The published accessibility statement claims automated accessibility testing and accessibility testing in the development process; the repo has neither a tool nor a CI job
findings.description: app/legal/accessibility/page.tsx:183-191 states the assessment approach as 'Self-evaluation using automated accessibility testing tools', 'Manual testing with screen readers and keyboard navigation' and 'Review against WCAG 2.1 success criteria', and :194-199 states 'we incorporate accessibility testing into our development process'. Neither package.json nor extension/package.json depends on axe, jest-axe, pa11y, lighthouse, jsdom, happy-dom or any testing-library package, and no workflow in .github/workflows/ references axe, a11y, accessibility or lighthouse. AUDIT-013#cov-09 already established that vitest.config.ts runs environment: node with no DOM, so no component can be rendered in a test at all, let alone audited. Two of the page's specific feature claims are checkable and split: the Skip Links claim at :92-95 is true (app/layout.tsx:175), while the Form Labels claim at :88-91 is already contradicted by AUDIT-011#docs-07 on the API playground.
findings.impact: This is a published legal accessibility statement, the document a regulator, a procurement reviewer or a complainant reads first. Two of its claims describe a process that provably does not exist in the repository, which turns a good-faith statement into an unsupported one and undermines the parts that are true.
findings.recommendation: Either make the claim true or narrow it. Adding jsdom plus @axe-core/react or a pa11y-ci pass over the main routes and one CI job is a day of work and would make both sentences accurate. If that is not on the roadmap, rewrite app/legal/accessibility/page.tsx:183-191 to describe what is actually done (manual keyboard and screen-reader passes, review against WCAG 2.1 AA) and delete the automated-tooling and 'incorporate accessibility testing into our development process' claims.

findings.title: HOST_BIND exists only as a comment inside docker-compose.yml, and the troubleshooting row for the exact symptom it causes points at APP_PORT instead
findings.description: docker-compose.yml:78 publishes the app as `"${HOST_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${APP_PORT:-3000}:3000"`, so out of the box the container is reachable only from the docker host itself. The only mention of the variable anywhere in the repository is the comment two lines above it at :76 ('Override with HOST_BIND=0.0.0.0 to expose'), repeated in docker-compose.dev.yml:68. HOST_BIND is not in .env.example, not in app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx, not in app/docs/setup/page.tsx, not in app/docs/config/page.tsx and not in README.md. app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:583-587 documents the symptom '502 from reverse proxy', cause 'App not listening on the expected port', fix 'Check APP_PORT (default 3000); confirm the app container is up via docker compose ps' and never mentions the bind address.
findings.impact: An operator whose reverse proxy, load balancer or LAN client is not on the docker host gets connection refused, follows the one troubleshooting row that matches the symptom, checks APP_PORT and `docker compose ps`, finds both correct, and has no documented next step. The variable that fixes it is discoverable only by reading the compose file.
findings.recommendation: Add HOST_BIND to .env.example beside APP_PORT with the 127.0.0.1 default and the 0.0.0.0 override spelled out, add it to the environment table on app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx, and extend the troubleshooting row at :583-587 to read 'Check HOST_BIND (default 127.0.0.1, set 0.0.0.0 if the proxy is not on this host) and APP_PORT (default 3000)'.

findings.title: Five product surfaces the README advertises have no documentation page: billing and subscription management, bulk scanning, notifications, admin operations, and what to do when a scan fails or reports nothing
findings.description: DOCS_NAV (components/docs/docs-nav.ts:13-140) has 19 entries across six sections. Cross-checking them against the shipped surface: (1) Billing. app/pricing, app/checkout, app/api/v3/billing/route.ts, app/api/v3/billing/subscription/cancel/route.ts and .../reactivate/route.ts exist, four paid plans are defined in lib/billing/catalog.ts, and three separate credit products have checkout components under components/billing/. No docs page explains plans, upgrading, cancelling, reactivating, credits, or what happens at the end of a trial; grepping app/docs for 'cancel' returns only API and team contexts and 'refund' returns one line on the AI page. (2) Bulk scanning. README.md:34 advertises it, app/api/v3/scan/bulk and components/scanner/dashboard-bulk-result.tsx implement it, and 'bulk scan' appears in app/docs only inside the API reference. (3) Notifications. app/api/v3/notifications exists and is referenced from eight docs pages in passing, with no page of its own. (4) Admin. app/admin plus 267 SETTINGS_REGISTRY entries, the audit log, impersonation, broadcasts, the Backup button and IP rules have no operator page; 'audit log' appears in app/docs only in the API reference and 'activity log' nowhere. (5) Troubleshooting a scan. Nothing anywhere covers a scan that fails, times out, or returns zero findings, which is the single most common support question for a scanner.
findings.impact: Every one of these lands in support instead of self-service, and the project has in-app support tickets (app/docs/triage covers them) so the cost is real. Billing is the sharpest: a paying user who wants to cancel has no documentation and must find the button, which is a chargeback and trust risk on a service with a real subscriber base.
findings.recommendation: Add three pages first, in this order: 'Plans and Billing' under Using VulnRadar (what each plan includes rendered from lib/billing/catalog.ts, how to upgrade, cancel and reactivate, how the three credit types work, what happens when a subscription lapses); 'Troubleshooting Scans' (timeouts, blocked targets, zero-finding results, robots.txt exclusions, what each terminal scan status means); and 'Administration' under Running your own (the /admin tabs, the settings registry, the audit log, backups, IP rules, impersonation). Fold bulk scanning into the scheduled-scans page or give it a section, and give notifications a section on the account-security page rather than a page of its own.

findings.title: middleware 301-redirects every request to https when X-Forwarded-Proto says http, with no environment opt-out, so a self-host behind a plain-HTTP reverse proxy is unreachable
findings.description: middleware.ts:219-229 reads the first value of X-Forwarded-Proto and, when it equals "http", rewrites the request URL's protocol to https: and returns a 301. There is no env flag guarding it: the only escape hatch in this file is DISABLE_CSP=1 (:252), which throws in production (:236-243) and in any case is checked after the redirect has already returned. The same assumption is baked into the security headers built at :131 and :161: `upgrade-insecure-requests` in the CSP and `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`, both emitted unconditionally on every response. Meanwhile docker-compose.yml:78 documents the plain-HTTP LAN case as supported: `- "${HOST_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${APP_PORT:-3000}:3000"` with the comment "Override with HOST_BIND=0.0.0.0 to expose the app port on all interfaces (e.g. bare metal LAN)", and app/docs/setup/page.tsx:283 tells operators to set NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=http://localhost:3000.
findings.impact: Direct access with no proxy is fine (no header, no redirect), so this only bites the configuration the self-hosting docs actually recommend: a reverse proxy in front. An operator running nginx or Traefik on an internal network, a Tailscale/VPN-only host, or a staging box without a certificate forwards X-Forwarded-Proto: http, the app 301s to https, the proxy has no TLS listener, and every request fails. The failure looks like a redirect loop or a connection refused with nothing in the app logs explaining it, and the operator has no supported way to turn it off short of editing middleware.ts and rebuilding, which the pinned-image Docker path (AUDIT-014#host-05) does not allow.
findings.recommendation: Gate the redirect on an explicit opt-out in middleware.ts:219: skip it when `process.env.ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP === "1"`, and skip the Strict-Transport-Security header and the CSP `upgrade-insecure-requests` directive in buildSecurityHeaders under the same flag. Document the variable in .env.example next to NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL and in app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx's TLS section, with an explicit warning that it is for trusted internal networks only. Keep the current behaviour as the default so nothing changes for the hosted instance.

findings.title: FOOTER_TEXT and BACKGROUND_COLOR_LIGHT are editable admin settings documented as branding knobs, but neither value is read by any rendering code: the footer prints a different literal and the light background colour is never emitted
findings.description: lib/config/registry.ts:515-523 registers FOOTER_TEXT with help "Short line rendered in the site footer", and :505-514 registers BACKGROUND_COLOR_LIGHT with help "Hex colour reported to the browser for light mode". Both have defaults from config-values.ts (CONFIG_FOOTER_TEXT at :191, CONFIG_BACKGROUND_COLOR_LIGHT at :190), and CONFIG_FOOTER_TEXT is listed to self-hosters as a branding value to edit at app/docs/config/page.tsx:249. Neither is exported from lib/config/constants.ts: greping app/, lib/ and components/ for FOOTER_TEXT and BACKGROUND_COLOR_LIGHT returns only lib/config/config-values.ts, lib/config/registry.ts, the docs page, and components/admin/features/settings-registry-utils.ts:149 (which gives FOOTER_TEXT a multiline textarea in the editor, so real UI work was done on a field nothing consumes). The actual footer line is a different literal built inline at components/scanner/footer.tsx:229-231: `{"\u00A9"} {new Date().getFullYear()} {APP_NAME}. For authorized security testing only.` The light background colour has no consumer either: app/layout.tsx:130 emits only `themeColor: BRANDING_PRIMARY_COLOR`, and app/manifest.ts:23 uses BRANDING_BACKGROUND_DARK for background_color, so nothing ever reads the light value.
findings.impact: Two settings that appear in the admin Branding tab, appear in the published configuration reference, validate their input (min/max length, a textarea affordance for one of them), save successfully, and do nothing at all. Unlike the rest of hc-01 these are not even fixable by editing config-values.ts and rebuilding, because no code path reads the constant either. An operator customising their fork's footer will change CONFIG_FOOTER_TEXT, rebuild, see the footer unchanged, and reasonably conclude the whole config system is broken.
findings.recommendation: Pick one direction per key. For FOOTER_TEXT: render it in components/scanner/footer.tsx:230 (export FOOTER_TEXT from lib/config/constants.ts alongside the other branding exports and use it in place of the hardcoded "For authorized ..." sentence, keeping the copyright line separate), or delete the registry entry at :515, the CONFIG_ constant at config-values.ts:191, the MULTILINE_SETTING_KEYS entry at settings-registry-utils.ts:149 and the docs bullet at app/docs/config/page.tsx:249. For BACKGROUND_COLOR_LIGHT: either emit it as a second themeColor entry with `media: "(prefers-color-scheme: light)"` in app/layout.tsx:130 (Next.js metadata supports an array of themeColor objects), or delete it the same way.

findings.title: NOREPLY_EMAIL is documented and registered as the From address on automated mail, but every outgoing email's From is SMTP_FROM || SMTP_USER and the NOREPLY_EMAIL constant is read by nothing
findings.description: lib/config/registry.ts:464-471 registers NOREPLY_EMAIL with help "From address on automated mail. Must be a domain your SMTP relay is allowed to send as." app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:153 tells self-hosters to set `export const CONFIG_NOREPLY_EMAIL = "noreply@yourdomain.com"` as part of the rebrand block, and app/docs/setup/page.tsx and app/docs/config/page.tsx:225 both list it. The actual From is built at lib/email/email.ts:430: `const from = `"${APP_NAME}" <${SMTP_FROM}>`;`, where SMTP_FROM is defined at lib/config/constants.ts:648-649 as `process.env.SMTP_FROM || process.env.SMTP_USER || SMTP_USER`. NOREPLY_EMAIL never appears in that path. The exported constant at lib/config/constants.ts:642 has zero readers anywhere in app/, lib/ or components/. The runtime setting has exactly two readers, and neither is a From address: app/api/v3/contact/route.ts:136 and app/api/v3/landing-contact/route.ts:101 use `await getSetting("NOREPLY_EMAIL")` as a reply-to fallback.
findings.impact: An operator who does exactly what /docs/self-hosting:153 tells them, or who edits the field in the admin Branding tab, changes nothing about who their users see mail from. Mail goes out as whatever SMTP_USER happens to be, which for a Gmail or SES relay is often a personal or IAM-shaped address rather than a no-reply alias. Worse, the registry help text specifically warns "Must be a domain your SMTP relay is allowed to send as", implying the operator can break delivery by getting it wrong, so someone debugging an SPF or DMARC rejection will spend time on a field that is not in the code path at all.
findings.recommendation: Make the From honour the setting: at lib/email/email.ts:430, resolve the address as `SMTP_FROM || (await getSetting("NOREPLY_EMAIL"))` (sendEmail is already async and server-only), so an explicit SMTP_FROM still wins for relays that require an exact envelope sender but the configured no-reply address is used otherwise. Then either delete the unused NOREPLY_EMAIL export at lib/config/constants.ts:642 or repoint it at the same resolution. If the SMTP_FROM-only behaviour is deliberate, instead rewrite the registry help at :470 and the two docs pages to say it is only used as a reply-to on contact-form acknowledgements.

findings.title: Five OpenRouter call sites hardcode https://vulnradar.dev in the HTTP-Referer header instead of importing APP_URL, and one also hardcodes the product name, so a self-hoster's AI spend is attributed to vulnradar.dev
findings.description: Five separate places build the OpenRouter attribution headers with a duplicated literal rather than the APP_URL export that already exists for exactly this: app/api/v3/ai/chat/route.ts:278, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:277, lib/ai/review-source.ts:204, lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:144 and lib/ai/verify-findings.ts:365, each `headers["HTTP-Referer"] = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "https://vulnradar.dev"`. lib/config/constants.ts:191 already resolves this as `export const APP_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL || CONFIG_APP_URL`, and four of these five files already import from that module. The duplication also drifts on the operator: `??` only falls through on null/undefined, so an operator who sets NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL to an empty string here gets an empty HTTP-Referer, whereas APP_URL's `||` would fall back. Separately, lib/ai/review-source.ts:205 sets `headers["X-Title"] = "VulnRadar"` as a bare literal while the other four use APP_NAME.
findings.impact: OpenRouter uses HTTP-Referer and X-Title for its public app rankings and for per-app spend attribution in the account dashboard. A self-hoster who configures AI_PROVIDER=openrouter with their own key has all of their traffic reported as coming from vulnradar.dev, and their GitHub repo-review traffic reported as the app "VulnRadar", so their own dashboard cannot distinguish their usage and a third party's product name appears on their bill's attribution. It also inflates vulnradar.dev's position on OpenRouter's rankings with traffic it did not generate. Small in money terms, wrong in every other sense, and it is the kind of thing a security-conscious self-hoster notices and files an issue about.
findings.recommendation: Replace all five with `APP_URL` imported from @/lib/config/constants (already imported in lib/ai/scan-summary.ts and lib/ai/verify-findings.ts; add the import in the other three), and replace the literal at lib/ai/review-source.ts:205 with APP_NAME to match its four siblings. Better still, extract one `openRouterAttributionHeaders()` helper into lib/ai/provider.ts, which already owns the per-provider base URL table at :113-114, and call it from all five so the sixth copy cannot be added.

findings.title: CHROME_WEB_STORE_URL and FIREFOX_ADDON_URL default to VulnRadar's own published listings despite a comment saying they are empty on a fork, so a fork's JSON-LD sameAs claims another organisation's store profiles
findings.description: lib/config/config-values.ts:144 carries the comment "Empty until a store listing is live for this fork/deployment" and is immediately followed at :145-146 by a non-empty Chrome Web Store URL for extension id nbmifpplhhejdfokaglpomdnbaifngfj, and at :149-150 by a non-empty Firefox AMO URL. components/seo/structured-data.tsx:70-80 relies on the stale comment's premise: its own comment says "Store URLs are empty on a fork that has not published one, so filter(Boolean) drops them cleanly", then builds `sameAs = [SEO_GITHUB_URL, DISCORD_INVITE_URL, CHROME_WEB_STORE_URL, FIREFOX_ADDON_URL].filter(Boolean)` and emits it in the JSON-LD Organization node at :95. filter(Boolean) drops nothing, because none of the four are empty. CONFIG_DISCORD_INVITE_URL at :143 is VulnRadar's own invite (discord.gg/...) and is rendered at components/landing/landing-open-source.tsx:59, components/profile/tabs/profile-social-tab.tsx:799 and app/llms.txt/route.ts:207. All three keys are `tier: "build"` in lib/config/registry.ts, so per hc-01 the admin panel cannot change them, and per AUDIT-014#host-05 the Docker path cannot rebuild to change them either.
findings.impact: A fork or self-hosted instance publishes structured data telling Google and every answer engine that its Organization's verified profiles include VulnRadar's Chrome Web Store listing, VulnRadar's Firefox add-on and VulnRadar's Discord server. That is a schema.org sameAs assertion of identity, not a link, so it actively merges the two entities in knowledge-graph terms, which is bad for both parties. The user-facing half is the same misdirection as hc-02: the fork's own footer and llms.txt point its users at a third party's community, and /docs/extension:113 and :139 send them to a store listing that only talks to vulnradar.dev.
findings.recommendation: Set CONFIG_CHROME_WEB_STORE_URL and CONFIG_FIREFOX_ADDON_URL to "" in lib/config/config-values.ts (making the comment at :144 true) and move the real hosted-instance values into NEXT_PUBLIC_CHROME_WEB_STORE_URL / NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREFOX_ADDON_URL env overrides read in lib/config/constants.ts:200-201, which is the pattern SEO_TWITTER_HANDLE and the verification tokens already use at :216-226. Do the same for CONFIG_DISCORD_INVITE_URL at :143. Then app/docs/extension/page.tsx should hide the store buttons when the URL is empty, and components/seo/structured-data.tsx's filter(Boolean) becomes the load-bearing guard its comment already claims it is.

findings.title: API_VERSION exists so "all API calls" can be switched between versions, but 60 fetch call sites across 28 files hardcode the /api/v3 path instead
findings.description: lib/config/client-constants.ts:80-83 declares `// API VERSION - Change this to switch all API calls between versions` followed by `export const API_VERSION = "v3"`, and :87 onwards builds the whole API route map from it as template literals. That map is used correctly 157 times across app/ and components/. It is also bypassed 60 times in 28 files by fetches that spell the version out: app/admin/page.tsx alone has five (:350, :447, :456, :468, :489), plus app/admin/ai-chats/[id]/page.tsx:73, app/checkout/browser-credits/page.tsx:35, app/checkout/credits/page.tsx:34, app/checkout/github-credits/page.tsx:36, app/checkout/[productId]/page.tsx:55, app/dashboard/page.tsx:273 and app/unsubscribe/page.tsx:197 among others. lib/config/config-values.ts:659-660 additionally exports CONFIG_API_CURRENT_VERSION and CONFIG_API_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS as a second, unconnected copy of the same fact.
findings.impact: The stated purpose of the constant is not achievable: bumping API_VERSION to v4 leaves 60 client calls pointed at v3, so the app would half-migrate with no compile error and no test failure, and the breakage would surface as scattered 404s in admin, checkout, dashboard and unsubscribe. This is the reverse-check shape the section is about: the operator or maintainer believes they changed one value and changed 72 percent of the call sites. Not self-host-breaking today, since v3 is the only supported version, but it makes the one migration the constant exists for unsafe.
findings.recommendation: Add the missing routes to the API map in lib/config/client-constants.ts:87 onwards (admin teams, admin updater status, ai conversations, ai info, auth me is already there, account unsubscribe) and replace the 60 literals with the map entries. Then add an ESLint `no-restricted-syntax` rule scoped to app/ and components/ that flags any string literal matching `/api/v\d`, so the 61st cannot be added silently. Also collapse CONFIG_API_CURRENT_VERSION into API_VERSION so there is one source of truth rather than two.

findings.title: The admin 'update password' action enforces a hardcoded 8-character minimum, bypassing the admin-configurable PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH (12) and the strength gate every user-facing path applies
findings.description: Every user-facing password path resolves the live setting and then runs the strength analyzer: app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:68-:72 and :88-:89, app/api/v3/auth/reset-password/route.ts:36-:41 and :46-:47, app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:316 and :301-:302, app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts:156 and :170-:171. All four call getSetting('PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH') (default CONFIG_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH = 12, lib/config/config-values.ts:314, admin-editable at lib/config/registry.ts:2130) and reject analyzePassword(pw).score < 3. The admin case 'update_password' at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:732-:753 does neither: it validates only `typeof newPassword !== 'string' || newPassword.length < 8`, hashes, writes, and revokes sessions. There is no getSetting call and no analyzePassword call anywhere in that branch.
findings.impact: On a deployment where the operator raised PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH to meet a policy, an admin resetting a user's password can still set an 8-character password, and 'Password123' passes because the analyzer never runs. The account then holds a credential the deployment's own configured policy forbids, and the audit log records it as a normal update_password action.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/admin/route.ts's update_password case, replace the literal 8 with `await getSetting('PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH')` and add the same `analyzePassword(newPassword).score < 3` rejection the other four routes use, so all five password write paths share one policy.

findings.title: Three transactional emails hardcode the expiry number in their body copy while the actual expiry is read from an admin-editable setting
findings.description: email2FACodeEmail(code) at lib/email/email.ts:1167-:1181 writes 'It expires in 10 minutes' at :1170 and :1176. The row it describes is inserted with `NOW() + ($4 * INTERVAL '1 minute')` where $4 is getSetting('EMAIL_2FA_CODE_EXPIRY_MINUTES') (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-send/route.ts:72-:74, app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:227-:230, app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:419-:421). The default is 10 (lib/config/config-values.ts:273) and the key is admin-editable at lib/config/registry.ts:2200. billingVerificationCodeEmail(code) at :1183-:1200 does the same with 'It expires in 5 minutes' (:1186, :1192) against BILLING_VERIFY_CODE_EXPIRY_MINUTES (default 5, config-values.ts:1220, registry.ts:894, read at app/api/v3/billing/verify/send/route.ts:61). teamInviteEmail(teamName, inviteLink, invitedBy) at :586-:609 says 'The invite expires in 7 days' (:598, :604) against TEAM_INVITE_EXPIRY_DAYS (default 7, config-values.ts:1042, registry.ts:2715, read at app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:209). None of the three template functions accepts an expiry parameter, so the copy cannot follow the setting.
findings.impact: An operator who tightens the 2FA code window to 5 minutes for a compliance requirement ships an email that tells every user it lasts 10, and users report the code 'expiring early' as a bug. The team-invite case is worse in the other direction: lengthen it to 30 days and recipients still see 'expires in 7 days' and discard a live invite.
findings.recommendation: Give each of the three templates an expiry argument (email2FACodeEmail(code, expiryMinutes), billingVerificationCodeEmail(code, expiryMinutes), teamInviteEmail(teamName, inviteLink, invitedBy, expiryDays)) and pass the value the call site already resolved for the INSERT. The call sites all have it in scope one line above.

findings.title: The Discord sign-in path hardcodes the email 2FA code expiry as SQL INTERVAL '10 minutes' while the other three insert sites read the admin setting
findings.description: Four code paths insert into email_2fa_codes.
