Everything else that is indexable is present: I diffed the 45 pageMetadata routes against PUBLIC_ROUTES and the docs nine are the entire gap. The generated surfaces do not have this problem because CHECK_ROUTES (line 80), CATEGORY_ROUTES (line 64) and ALTERNATIVE_ROUTES (line 72) derive from the same loaders the pages use.
findings.impact: Nine documentation pages, including /docs/cli (the page AUDIT-013#subdeps-01 flags for advertising `npx vulnradar`), /docs/github, /docs/teams and /docs/triage, are absent from the file search engines use to prioritise crawling, and carry no lastmod or priority signal. They are reachable by internal link so they will eventually be found, but they are crawled last and refreshed slowest, which is exactly backwards for the pages that answer high-intent product questions. The stated invariant of the file is also false, which means the next docs page added will silently repeat this.
findings.recommendation: In lib/seo/routes.ts, delete the eleven hand-typed `/docs*` entries and derive them: `import { DOCS_PAGES } from "@/components/docs/docs-nav";` then `const DOCS_ROUTES: readonly PublicRoute[] = DOCS_PAGES.map((p) => ({ path: p.href, priority: p.href === "/docs" ? 0.8 : 0.7, changeFrequency: "monthly" as const }));` and spread DOCS_ROUTES into PUBLIC_ROUTES alongside CHECK_ROUTES. That makes the docs sitemap entries as drift-proof as the check ones and matches the file's own stated design. docs-nav.ts is a plain data module with no client-only imports, so importing it from lib/seo/routes.ts is safe.

findings.title: Every docs child page emits two conflicting TechArticle blocks and two conflicting BreadcrumbList blocks, one pair from the parent layout describing /docs instead of the current page
findings.description: app/docs/layout.tsx renders BreadcrumbStructuredData with items [{ name: "Docs", path: "/docs" }] at line 32 and TechArticleStructuredData with title "Documentation" and path "/docs" at line 36, both outside DocsShell and therefore on every route beneath /docs. Each of the 19 child sections then renders its own pair: app/docs/cli/layout.tsx:28 emits BreadcrumbList [Docs, CLI] and line 35 emits TechArticle with url /docs/cli. So the HTML for /docs/cli carries two `application/ld+json` BreadcrumbList blocks (one a single-item trail pointing at the wrong page) and two TechArticle blocks whose `url` and `headline` disagree. The same shape exists under legal: app/legal/layout.tsx:28 emits BreadcrumbList [Legal] on every legal route, and app/legal/terms/layout.tsx:24 emits [Legal, Terms of Service] on top of it. That is 19 docs pages plus 6 legal pages carrying contradictory structured data. Separately, the child breadcrumbs start at "Docs" or "Legal" with no "Home" position 1, while the /checks pages correctly start at Home (app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:146).
findings.impact: When a page publishes two BreadcrumbList items Google treats them as alternative trails and may render either, so a docs result can show the trail "Docs" with no leaf, or nothing. Two TechArticle blocks with different `url` values on one page is the malformed case: the parent block asserts that this page is the /docs index, which contradicts the canonical the same page sets. It is exactly the sort of inconsistency that makes a validator flag the page and makes Google discard the markup rather than pick a winner, so all 25 pages lose the rich-result eligibility the markup was added for.
findings.recommendation: Move both JSON-LD blocks out of app/docs/layout.tsx into app/docs/page.tsx, so the /docs index describes itself and no child inherits them. Do the same for app/legal/layout.tsx into app/legal/page.tsx. Then prepend `{ name: "Home", path: "/landing" }` to the items array in all 19 docs child layouts and all 6 legal child layouts so the trail matches the /checks convention at app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:145-150. If the shared trail is worth keeping DRY, add a `docsBreadcrumb(leafLabel, leafPath)` helper next to DOCS_NAV that returns [Home, Docs, leaf] and call it from each child.

findings.title: The check-count sentence appended to every /checks category description is silently deleted again by the clamp on 17 of the 18 categories, so the one number that differentiates those pages never reaches the meta description
findings.description: app/checks/category/[category]/page.tsx:64 sets description = clampText(`${seo.intro} ${count} checks, each with fix steps and code.`). The comment above it (lines 59-61) says the clamp exists because "several category intros are long enough that appending the count sentence pushed them past 160". I ran clampText (lib/seo/metadata.ts:19) over all 18 CATEGORY_SEO intros in lib/seo/checks-content.ts:188: 17 of the 18 lose the appended sentence completely, and 17 of the 18 end in "...". Only `reputation` (a 139-character intro) survives, and it is the only one that keeps "3 checks, each with fix steps and code." The concatenation order guarantees this: the intros are 130 to 160 characters on their own, so a 39-character suffix appended before a 155-character clamp can never survive.
findings.impact: The eighteen category pages are the mid-tier of the SEO surface, sitting between /checks and the 749 leaves, and the only thing that differentiates their snippet from the on-page intro copy is the check count. Every one of those snippets is instead a truncated version of the intro, ending in an ellipsis. Google may then substitute its own snippet from the body, which defeats the point of writing intros tuned for the meta window at all.
findings.recommendation: Reorder the concatenation at app/checks/category/[category]/page.tsx:62-65 so the differentiator survives: `description: clampText(`${count} ${label.toLowerCase()} checks, each with fix steps and code. ${seo.intro}`)`. That leads with the number, keeps the whole count clause, and lets the intro be the part that clamps. Alternatively clamp the intro to `155 - suffix.length` first and then append. Assert in a test that all 18 rendered descriptions contain the digit count, so the regression cannot recur.

findings.title: The security badge is the product's only backlink loop and every badge points at a /shared/ URL that is Disallowed in robots.txt and served noindex, nofollow, so the inbound links are thrown away
findings.description: app/docs/sharing/page.tsx:386 publishes the embed snippet users paste onto their own sites: ``. Both halves of that snippet point at paths that robots.txt forbids: `/shared/` via lib/seo/routes.ts:121 and `/api/` via line 108, both spread into the wildcard Disallow at app/robots.ts:60. On top of that the link target itself serves `noindex, nofollow` (app/shared/[token]/layout.tsx:7 via privatePageMetadata, lib/seo/metadata.ts:85). So the destination cannot be crawled, cannot be indexed, and carries nofollow. The image is an SVG served from /api/v3/badge/[token] (app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:122, Content-Type image/svg+xml), which is also Disallowed and which social and image crawlers do not render.
findings.impact: A security badge on a customer's site is the standard organic-growth loop for this product category: it is how Security Headers, SSL Labs and Mozilla Observatory accumulate their link graph. Here the feature is built, documented, and produces a link that search engines are explicitly told to ignore. Every customer who installs a badge gives the product a link worth nothing.
findings.recommendation: Point the documented `<a href>` at `/host/<hostname>` instead of `/shared/<token>`: it is the stable, per-host public page for the same site (app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts only ever serves public scans, and its host_reputation row is deleted when a scan is made private), it does not expose a token in someone else's page source, and it is the page a stranger arriving from the badge actually wants. Then do seo-09 so that target is indexable and followable. Update the snippet at app/docs/sharing/page.tsx:386 and anywhere the badge UI generates the same HTML. Keep the SVG badge image where it is; the link, not the image, is what carries the value.

findings.title: /host/[hostname] is kept noindex and robots-Disallowed on the stated grounds that the URL space is "not enumerable", which is false: host_reputation is a table and /public-scans already paginates it
findings.description: lib/seo/routes.ts:100-106 justifies excluding /host/ and /shared/ together: "Tokenised or per-entity URLs (/shared/<token>, /browser/<id>, /host/<hostname>). Not enumerable ahead of time, so there is no fixed list to publish a sitemap entry or canonical for." That reasoning is correct for /shared/<token> and /browser/<id>, which are secrets. It is not correct for /host/<hostname>: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts:99 reads from the `host_reputation` table keyed on `host`, so the full list is a single SELECT, and app/public-scans/page.tsx already renders a paginated, sitemapped, indexable directory of exactly this data. The data is public by construction, not by accident: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts:140 gates the live findings on `is_public = true`, and the route's own comment states the host_reputation row is deleted when its source scan is made private. The page also already has a per-host trend chart (components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx). Today the page ships privatePageMetadata("Host Report", "/host") (app/host/[hostname]/layout.tsx:8), so it has no per-host title, no per-host description, a canonical pointing at /host which is not a route, and noindex.
findings.impact: "<domain> security report" and "is <domain> safe" are the highest-volume query shapes in this product category, and they are the entire organic strategy of Security Headers, SSL Labs, Mozilla Observatory and urlscan.io. The product already generates the pages that answer them, already restricts them to public data, already links them from an indexable directory, and then blocks all of them. The 749 /checks pages target "how to fix X" intent, which converts worse: someone searching a check name is fixing a problem they already found, while someone searching a domain is looking for a scanner.
findings.recommendation: Three changes. (1) Replace app/host/[hostname]/layout.tsx with an async generateMetadata({ params }) that resolves the host via the same host_reputation lookup and returns pageMetadata({ title: `${host} security report`, description: `${host} scored ${dangerScore}/10 on ${date}: ${critical} critical and ${high} high findings across headers, TLS, cookies and DNS.`, path: `/host/${host}`, noIndex: !known || findings.length === 0 }), so an unscanned or empty host stays noindex and only real reports are indexable. (2) Remove "/host/" from DISALLOWED_PATHS in lib/seo/routes.ts:122, leaving "/shared/" and "/browser/" in place. (3) Publish the URLs: add a second sitemap (Next 15 supports generateSitemaps(), or a plain app/sitemap-hosts.xml/route.ts) that selects host and last_scanned_at from host_reputation and emits a real per-host lastmod, and reference both from a sitemap index. Note app/sitemap.ts is currently `force-static` so the host sitemap must be a separate dynamic route. Pair with seo-02 so each host page also gets a real social card, and with seo-08 so badges point here.

findings.title: The 749 check pages call generateStaticParams and produce zero prerendered HTML, so the entire organic surface is an uncacheable per-request render and Cloudflare returns a MISS on 100 percent of crawler traffic
findings.description: This is the SEO quantification of AUDIT-012#fe-01 and AUDIT-012#perf-17 (root cause: app/layout.tsx:146 awaits headers() for the CSP nonce, which opts every segment beneath it into per-request dynamic rendering). Do not re-file the root cause. What matters for section 19 is the shape of the loss. app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:34 exports generateStaticParams() returning all 749 check ids, and the file's own comment at lines 29-31 states it produces nothing: "The root layout reads headers() for its CSP nonce, so the whole app already renders per-request." app/checks/category/[category]/page.tsx:27 and app/alternatives/[competitor]/page.tsx:17 do the same. AUDIT-012#fe-01 measured the committed build: .next/prerender-manifest.json lists exactly 5 prerendered routes (robots.txt, sitemap.xml, manifest.webmanifest, llms.txt, llms-full.txt) against 311 app-build-manifest entries, and Next sets `cache-control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` on dynamically rendered app pages. The sitemap I computed from lib/seo/routes.ts contains 805 URLs: 33 hand-listed, 18 categories, 5 alternatives, 749 checks. Every one is an origin React render with an uncacheable response, on the same single Node process that runs scans. No route sets `revalidate`, so there is no ISR fallback either. On top of that, AUDIT-012#fe-02 measured that the root-layout ChatWidget puts react-markdown plus remark-gfm (144 KB raw / 44 KB gzipped) and an /api/v3/ai/info request on all 311 routes, and AUDIT-011#docs-05 measured /checks at ~190 KB of HTML for 754 list items.
findings.impact: Crawl budget is spent on origin CPU rather than edge bytes: a full Googlebot pass over the sitemap is 805 cold server-side renders, each also serving a JS bundle Googlebot must parse in its rendering pass, with a Cache-Control header that forbids both the CDN and Googlebot's own cache from reusing anything on the next crawl. Nothing in this repo can be measured for TTFB here (no build, no deploy, no Docker on this machine), but the mechanism is unambiguous: the HTML cache hit rate on the organic surface is structurally zero, and content that is byte-identical between deploys is regenerated for every crawler hit and every visitor. Crawler traffic also directly competes with scan execution for the same CPU, so an organic traffic spike degrades the product.
findings.recommendation: Separate the SEO surface from the nonce. Move the public content routes (/checks, /checks/category, /alternatives, /tools, /docs, /legal, /landing, /pricing) into a route group such as app/(marketing)/ with its own layout.tsx that does NOT call headers(), and lift the inline auth-cache script out of the root layout for that group (it is only useful to signed-in users, who are not on these pages). Those routes then prerender from their existing generateStaticParams and become CDN-cacheable. Because the inline script's content is deterministic (it is built from STAFF_ROLES at build time), the alternative fix is a hash-based CSP for that one script, which lets the root layout drop headers() entirely. Either way, add `export const revalidate = 86400` to the check and category routes so a content edit still reaches the edge without a deploy. Verify by checking that .next/prerender-manifest.json lists the 749 check routes after the change.

findings.title: /public-scans is an indexable, hourly-priority sitemap entry whose server HTML is a loading skeleton and whose every outbound link is robots-Disallowed and noindex, nofollow
findings.description: lib/seo/routes.ts:45 registers /public-scans in the sitemap at priority 0.6 with changeFrequency "hourly", and app/public-scans/layout.tsx gives it real indexable metadata ("Public Scans: Shared Reports Directory"). The page itself is app/public-scans/page.tsx:1 "use client": it fetches the listing from API.PUBLIC_SCANS in a useEffect with `loading` initialised true, so the server-rendered HTML a crawler receives is PublicScansTableSkeleton (lines 23-38), eight rows of grey placeholders and no scan data. The only link out of each row is components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:21, `href={`/shared/${scan.token}`}`, and /shared/ is Disallowed in robots.txt (app/robots.ts:60 via lib/seo/routes.ts:121) and served noindex, nofollow (app/shared/[token]/layout.tsx:7). So the page tells crawlers it changes hourly, delivers no content without JS, and points every one of its links at a URL they are forbidden to follow.
findings.impact: The hourly changeFrequency asks Google to re-crawl a page that is byte-identical on every fetch, which is exactly the signal Google penalises as unreliable and then ignores for the whole sitemap. The directory contributes nothing to the index: no scan URLs, no host names, no verdicts, and no crawlable outbound links, despite being the one page on the site whose content is fresh, unique and query-shaped ("is example.com safe"). It is a sitemap entry that consumes crawl budget and returns an empty page.
findings.recommendation: Make the listing server-rendered: split app/public-scans/page.tsx into a server component that awaits the same query app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts runs and passes the first page as a prop, with the existing client component taking over for pagination (the client already syncs `?page=` via url-state). Change the row link at components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:21 from `/shared/${scan.token}` to `/host/${hostname}` so the directory links to the crawlable per-host page (see seo-09) instead of a token URL; keep the token link for the owner's own view if needed. Lower changeFrequency in lib/seo/routes.ts:45 from "hourly" to "daily", which is closer to true for a 50-user service.

findings.title: The five SoftwareApplication JSON-LD blocks carry no offers, aggregateRating or review, so none is eligible for Google's software rich result, and /pricing (the only page with prices) emits no SoftwareApplication at all
findings.description: SoftwareStructuredData (components/seo/structured-data.tsx:130) accepts an `offers` array and emits an Offer list at lines 165-175. Grepping every call site: app/landing/page.tsx:109, app/demo/layout.tsx:27, app/tools/page.tsx:50, app/tools/api-scanner/page.tsx:71 and app/tools/link-checker/page.tsx:73. All five pass only `nonce`, so the offers branch is unreachable and every emitted block has no offers, no aggregateRating and no review. Google's Software App structured-data requirements list `name` plus at least one of `offers`, `aggregateRating` or `review` as required for the rich result, so all five blocks are ineligible. Meanwhile app/pricing/layout.tsx renders only FaqStructuredData (line 47), no SoftwareApplication, even though lib/billing/plans.ts already exposes getPaidPlans() with priceInCents and the layout already imports it at line 14 to compute CHEAPEST_PAID. Two secondary defects in the same block: the five copies have no `@id`, so five pages assert five unlinked entities with the same `name` and `url: APP_URL`; and `license: SEO_LICENSE` (line 150) is the string "GPL-3.0" where schema.org expects a CreativeWork or a URL. Also worth noting: the blocks on /tools/api-scanner and /tools/link-checker describe the whole product with a featureList of 795+ checks on pages that are about one single free tool.
findings.impact: The pricing panel with a price and a Free badge in the search result, which is the visible payoff of SoftwareApplication markup and the reason this component exists, can never render for any page. The markup is written, maintained, and shipped on five pages, and Google discards all of it. Five duplicate unlinked entities also make it harder for answer engines to resolve "VulnRadar" to one thing, which is the same problem the Organization @id at line 62 was added to solve.
findings.recommendation: Add `<SoftwareStructuredData nonce={nonce} offers={[{ name: "Free", priceInCents: 0 }, ...getPaidPlans().map(p => ({ name: p.name, priceInCents: p.priceInCents }))]} />` to app/pricing/layout.tsx, gated on BILLING_ENABLED so a self-host with billing off does not publish prices. Give the block a stable `"@id": `${APP_URL}/#software`` in components/seo/structured-data.tsx and have the other four call sites emit `{ "@type": "SoftwareApplication", "@id": SOFTWARE_ID }` as a reference instead of a full duplicate. Change `license` to the SPDX URL `https://spdx.org/licenses/GPL-3.0-or-later.html` (add a CONFIG_SEO_LICENSE_URL next to CONFIG_SEO_LICENSE in lib/config/config-values.ts:245 so a fork can change it). Do not fabricate an aggregateRating: `offers` alone satisfies the requirement.

findings.title: The /checks pages are thin: 363 of 749 carry under 100 words of unique body copy, and the FAQ block on every one of them is the same four templated questions restating text already on the page
findings.description: I measured unique body copy per check page as description plus riskImpact plus explanation plus fixSteps, over all 749 entries getAllChecks() returns. Median is 101 words. 712 of 749 are under 200 words and 363 are under 100. The thinnest are /checks/webauthn-usage at 14 words, /checks/docker-hub-token-exposed at 15, /checks/permissions-policy-usb-blocked at 16. 643 of 749 have exactly one code example and 160 have exactly one fix step. 293 of the 749 share one of just three identical `references` arrays (137 pages share one OWASP XSS pair, 99 share one secure-headers pair, 57 share a third). On top of that, app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:89 buildFaq() generates the same four questions on all 749 pages (`What is "<title>"?`, `How do I fix <title>?`, `How severe is <title>?`, `Which standards does <title> map to?`) and answers them with check.description, check.fixSteps.join(" ") and check.riskImpact, all three of which are already rendered verbatim higher up the same page (lines 199, 210, 228-238). So the FAQ section, and the FaqStructuredData built from it at line 160, is a second copy of the page body on every page.
findings.impact: A set of 749 pages that share a template, a title prefix, three reference lists and an identical four-question FAQ, with a median of 101 words of genuinely unique text, is the pattern Google's helpful-content and thin-affiliate guidance targets. The risk is set-wide rather than per-page: a site-level quality signal suppresses all 749 at once, which would take out the entire organic strategy. Duplicating the body text into an FAQ also makes the pages look longer to a word count while adding nothing a reader did not already read.
findings.recommendation: Vary the template, not just the data. Per page, add sections whose content is necessarily unique: (1) "What VulnRadar looks for" naming the actual response header, cookie attribute, DNS record, file path or regex the detector matches, which is already in lib/scanner/checks/* and lib/scanner/checks-data/*.json under `evidence`/`type` and is discarded by normalise() at lib/seo/checks-content.ts:102; (2) "How to verify the fix" with a concrete curl or dig command derived from the check category, which is templatable per category rather than per check and still gives 18 distinct shapes; (3) severity rationale, one sentence saying why this is high and not medium. Replace buildFaq's four generic questions with two or three drawn from the same per-check data but not restated elsewhere on the page, and drop any question whose answer is verbatim body text (the `How do I fix` one especially, which is fixSteps.join(" ")). Widen the three shared reference lists so a page's references are specific to its check. Prioritise the 363 pages under 100 words: for the ones that cannot be given real depth (single Permissions-Policy directives, for example), fold them into their category page and 301 the leaf, rather than shipping a 14-word page.

findings.title: The GitHub Action gate stops at severity counts and never uploads the SARIF the API already produces, so findings never reach the Security tab that ZAP, Nuclei and Snyk actions all populate
findings.description: The composite action at .github/actions/scan-gate/action.yml is complete and correct: it starts a scan, polls GET /scan/status, and at :152 to :176 reads only summary.critical/high/medium/low/total, writes a step summary table, and exits 1 on threshold breach. It never fetches SARIF. A full SARIF 2.1.0 generator already exists at lib/reports/sarif-report.ts:1 and is exposed as GET /api/v3/history/[id]/report?format=sarif (app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts:174), and app/docs/reports/page.tsx:310 to :319 already publishes the exact two-step recipe (curl the SARIF, then github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3) as something the user must hand-assemble. The action already emits scan-id as an output (.github/actions/scan-gate/action.yml:45), so the two halves are one curl apart. Separately, the action lives at .github/actions/scan-gate/ inside the app repo, which is not a GitHub Marketplace-publishable location: Marketplace requires action.yml at the root of its own repository plus a tagged release. ZAP ships official Marketplace actions, Nuclei ships one, and Snyk and Burp both list Actions integrations (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors.md, ZAP and Nuclei sections).
findings.impact: A developer wiring VulnRadar into CI gets a red X and a markdown table, while the equivalent ZAP or Nuclei action gets them annotated Code Scanning alerts inline on the pull-request diff, with dismissal and tracking handled by GitHub. That is the difference between a gate people keep and a gate people delete after the second false alarm. And because the action is not on the Marketplace, the highest-intent discovery channel for this product (a developer searching the Actions marketplace for "security scan") returns nothing.
findings.recommendation: Two changes, both small. First, in .github/actions/scan-gate/action.yml add an optional `sarif-file` input (default `vulnradar.sarif`); after the poll loop succeeds, curl `$VR_API_BASE/history/$scan_id/report?format=sarif` to that path and add a `sarif-file` output, then document the follow-on `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` step in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1299's snippet so the published example is the complete one. Second, mirror the action into a dedicated `VulnRadar/scan-gate-action` repo with action.yml at the root and a v1 tag, publish it to the Marketplace, and change the `uses:` in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1299 from the current `${APP_REPO}/.github/actions/scan-gate@main` (an unpinned branch reference) to `VulnRadar/scan-gate-action@v1`.

findings.title: There is no overall A+ to F grade, so the badge and public host report speak safe/caution/unsafe and cannot occupy the vocabulary SecurityHeaders.com just vacated
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 3: the grading vocabulary and the badge flywheel
findings.description: Four of the free peers grade a whole site on one A+ to F scale: MDN HTTP Observatory (A+ down to F, ten header tests), SecurityHeaders.com (A+ to F on response headers), Qualys SSL Labs (A+ to F plus T and M), and ImmuniWeb (grade-gated PDF certificate plus installable badge). VulnRadar has the scoring machinery but not the vocabulary. lib/scanner/ssl-grade.ts:1 already computes a real SSL-Labs-style A+/A/B/C/D/F letter, but only for the TLS handshake. The whole-scan verdict is a three-state safety rating (lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts:19, "safe" | "caution" | "unsafe") plus a 0-10 danger score (:306), and the embeddable badge renders exactly that three-state label (app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:99 to :115). Confirmed live this session: Snyk shut down the securityheaders.com API in April 2026 (announced January 2026), leaving only the free web scanner; the replacements ranking for "securityheaders alternative" are unknown micro-vendors (WebAudit, Guardr, detectzestack, myssl.info, sitesecurityscore). SSL Labs v4 requires an organizational email and forbids commercial use by default, and MDN Observatory dropped TLS entirely in October 2024. The auto-updating badge infrastructure already exists and is idempotent per (user, url) so an embed never breaks (app/api/v3/badge/site/route.ts:8).
findings.impact: A README badge that says "caution" is a liability the owner removes; a badge that says "A" is a trophy the owner keeps and that links back. ImmuniWeb built 380M+ scans on exactly that mechanic and gates the certificate on the grade so people work to earn it. VulnRadar has the badge, the public host page, the API, and TLS plus DNS plus header coverage that the vacated SecurityHeaders niche wants, and cannot be compared against the incumbent because it does not speak the incumbent's scale.
findings.recommendation: Add `getSiteGrade(findings): "A+"|"A"|"B"|"C"|"D"|"F"` to lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts, derived from the existing danger score and severity weights so it stays deterministic and needs no new detection work, and document the exact deduction table on a public page the way lib/scanner/ssl-grade.ts:20 already documents its own. Render the grade as the primary label in app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:99 (keep safe/caution/unsafe as the badge's secondary colour semantics), lead with it on app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx, and gate the shareable badge on B or better, matching ImmuniWeb. Then publish a keyless or free-key-tier grading endpoint documented in app/docs/api as the drop-in for the dead securityheaders.com API, using the existing demo-scan rate-limit shape (app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:97) rather than the account-gated /api/v3/scan.

findings.title: The /alternatives set names five competitors, one of which stopped existing as a standalone product in November 2024, and omits every free-tool and open-source peer the product actually competes with
findings.description: lib/seo/alternatives.ts:53 defines exactly five entries: intelliradar (:55), detectify (:108), intruder (:162), probely (:215) and qualys (:268). Each renders a public page at /alternatives/<slug> (app/alternatives/[competitor]/page.tsx:18) and is listed in lib/seo/routes.ts:72. Two problems. First, the Probely entry at :215 to :266 describes Probely in the present tense as an independent commercial vendor; Probely was acquired by Snyk on 12 November 2024 and relaunched as "Snyk API and Web" on 22 April 2025, with help.probely.com now titled "Snyk API and Web Help Center" (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors-commercial.md, Probely section, verified live). Second, the set is aimed entirely at commercial DAST vendors the product does not realistically win against on features, and contains none of the peers it actually shares a shape with: SecurityHeaders.com, MDN HTTP Observatory, SSL Labs, ImmuniWeb, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, or the cheapest credible paid entries (Pentest-Tools.com from $95/mo, Astra from $69/mo). The one entry with no real competitor behind it, "IntelliRadar" (:55), is filler whose comparison rows all say "Varies by product" (:66, :72, :76, :81, :87).
findings.impact: A live public page tells visitors to compare VulnRadar against a product that no longer sells under that name, which is the kind of staleness that gets screenshotted and undermines the page's own stated ground rule at lib/seo/alternatives.ts:1 to :13 that only defensible facts appear. Meanwhile the highest-intent search terms available right now, "securityheaders.com alternative" and "securityheaders api alternative" (a well-known free API that died four months ago, with only unknown micro-vendors ranking), have no page at all.
findings.recommendation: In lib/seo/alternatives.ts: rename the probely entry to slug "snyk" / name "Snyk API and Web", note the Probely lineage in one sentence of `summary`, and keep /alternatives/probely alive as a redirect so existing links and sitemap entries do not 404. Delete or replace the intelliradar entry, whose rows carry no information. Add entries for securityheaders (lead with: the API shut down in April 2026, VulnRadar's covers headers plus TLS plus DNS plus cookies in one call), mozilla-observatory (lead with: dropped TLS entirely in October 2024), ssl-labs (lead with: v4 requires a corporate email and forbids commercial use, VulnRadar computes its own grade in lib/scanner/ssl-grade.ts), owasp-zap and nuclei (be honest: they send deeper payloads, VulnRadar is the hosted zero-setup path with a public check catalog), and pentest-tools (the closest analogue in shape, and the cheapest credible paid rival at $95/mo against VulnRadar's $5 to $20).

findings.title: Authenticated scanning ships form, header and cookie login but no recorded multi-step sequence, no TOTP, no SSO/OIDC login, and no re-authentication when the target drops the session mid-scan
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 5: authenticated scanning, narrowed against the code
findings.description: The research called authenticated scanning the single biggest gap and flagged it for verification. Verified in code, the gap is much narrower than that. lib/scanner/auth/types.ts:13 declares `ScanAuthType = "form" | "header" | "cookie"`, all three are implemented (lib/scanner/auth/login.ts, lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts), and the form path is better than a naive implementation: it opens a real headless browser session to render a client-side login form before parsing it (lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts:1 to :27). POST /api/v3/scan/authenticated exists (app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:56), the session is origin-bound with a logout guard (lib/scanner/auth/scan-session.ts:104 to :113), and the crawl engine reports the auth state back. What is genuinely absent: (1) multi-step or recorded login sequences, a browser-recorder capture of the click path (Detectify ships a Chrome recorder, Astra uses Chrome DevTools Recorder, Pentest-Tools and Acunetix both ship a login sequence recorder, Snyk supports recorded sequences); (2) TOTP or OTP second factor, which Astra and Snyk both handle and Acunetix explicitly claims for MFA and CAPTCHA; (3) SSO or OpenID Connect login flows, which only Snyk supports; (4) automatic re-authentication when the session dies mid-scan. On (4), lib/scanner/auth/scan-session.ts:86 `markLost()` records the loss and :116 to :154 detects all three loss signals (cleared session cookie, 401/403, redirect back to the login path), but nothing ever calls establishScanSession again: a grep for re-auth, reauth, relogin across lib/scanner/ and app/api/v3/scan/ returns zero hits. Snyk is the only one of the eight with automatic re-auth mid-scan.
findings.impact: For this product's users (developers scanning their own staging app behind a login) the practical bite is ordered opposite to the market's marketing. Item (4) costs users today: a long crawl of a session-expiring app silently degrades to an anonymous scan partway through and reports status "lost", so the user pays a scan against their daily quota and gets a partial result they must re-run by hand. Items (1) to (3) cost the product a specific class of prospect (SPAs with a multi-screen login, any team with 2FA enforced on staging) but each is expensive to build and none is a same-day fix.
findings.recommendation: Build (4) first, alone: it is the smallest change and the only one costing users today. In lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts, when the binding reports `lost`, call `establishScanSession` once more with the same EphemeralAuthInput held in memory for that request, cap re-auth at two attempts per scan, and record the count in ScanAuthReport (lib/scanner/auth/types.ts:85) so the result says "re-authenticated once" rather than "lost". Then add TOTP as (2): it is a `totpSecret` field on EphemeralFormAuth (lib/scanner/auth/types.ts:21), an otpauth-style code generator, and one extra form submit in lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts, and it unlocks every target with authenticator-app 2FA. Defer (1) recorded sequences and (3) SSO: a recorder needs a browser extension capture format, a step-replay engine on top of the BrowserBase CDP path, and stored (not ephemeral) sequence definitions, which contradicts the deliberate never-persisted credential model documented at lib/scanner/auth/types.ts:1 to :10. That model is itself an advantage worth keeping; see comp-10.

findings.title: SARIF ships but nothing connects it to DefectDojo or Faraday, the two open-source vulnerability managers this product's self-hosting users already run
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 6: OSS ecosystem interop
findings.description: DefectDojo (4,911 stars, BSD-3-Clause, 500+ report parsers, actively pushed 2026-08-29) is the layer OSS-first teams aggregate scanners into, and it already parses ZAP, Nuclei, Trivy, Nikto, Burp, SSL Labs and Wapiti; Faraday (6,697 stars, GPL-3.0, 80+ tool plugins) is the same shape (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors.md, DefectDojo and Faraday sections, both verified live). VulnRadar already emits everything such a parser needs: a complete SARIF 2.1.0 report with per-rule descriptors, security-severity, tags and helpUri (lib/reports/sarif-report.ts:1 to :253), reachable over the API at GET /api/v3/history/[id]/report?format=sarif (app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts:174). Nothing in the repo, the docs (app/docs/reports/page.tsx), or .github/ mentions DefectDojo, Faraday, or any vulnerability-management destination. The word appears nowhere in the codebase.
findings.impact: The self-hosting, GPL, small-security-team audience is precisely the DefectDojo audience, and it is also the audience most likely to install a second scanner rather than switch. Being absent from the 500-parser list means VulnRadar is the one tool in their stack whose findings have to be moved by hand, which is how a tool gets dropped at the next cleanup.
findings.recommendation: Two cheap moves. First, add a "Send findings to DefectDojo" subsection to app/docs/reports/page.tsx next to the existing SARIF and CI section (:279), showing the curl that pulls SARIF and POSTs it to DefectDojo's /api/v2/import-scan/ endpoint with scan_type=SARIF, which already works today with zero code change. Second, open a parser PR upstream to DefectDojo (a ~150-line Python parser plus fixtures) that reads VulnRadar's native JSON export so the tool is named in their supported list; that listing is a durable discovery channel that costs one afternoon.

findings.title: The 750 public check pages have no contribute-a-check path, leaving the one moat a GPL scanner can actually build (the nuclei-templates model) unstarted
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 7 and list (b): the community check catalog
findings.description: nuclei-templates carries roughly 11,997 template files across 873 directories with daily commits, a formal Pioneers program, and template bounties; that community, not the binary, is the moat none of the commercial eight have (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors.md, Nuclei section, verified live). VulnRadar has the raw material: a per-category registry with static JSON check definitions (lib/scanner/registry.ts:23 to :40, 18 categories), a public page per check, and an index at app/checks/page.tsx:75 whose own copy says "Not a marketing number: every one is a real page that tells you what it catches". It also already has a well-designed Scanner Detector Proposal issue template (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/detector.md:1) asking for threat model, detection strategy, false-positive risk and test fixtures. None of that is connected: grep for "detector.md", "Propose" or "contribute" across app/checks/ and components/checks/ returns zero hits, so no visitor to any of the ~750 pages is ever told a check can be proposed. AGENTS.md:140 to :167 documents the add-a-check procedure for maintainers only, and CONTRIBUTING.md (56 lines) never mentions checks at all.
findings.impact: The check catalog is simultaneously the main organic SEO surface and the only asset that compounds without headcount, and it currently converts zero readers into contributors. A security-minded reader who lands on a check page from a search, spots a gap, and finds no way in leaves. Every commercial peer's detection set is closed; VulnRadar's is open and unadvertised, which is the worst of both.
findings.recommendation: Add a persistent block to app/checks/page.tsx below the category accordion (:140) and to the bottom of app/checks/[id]/page.tsx: a two-line pitch plus a direct link to the prefilled issue template at https://github.com/{APP_REPO}/issues/new?template=detector.md, and a link to a new app/docs/developers section that walks the actual change (add a def to lib/scanner/checks-data/<category>.json, add a detector to lib/scanner/checks/<category>.ts, run scripts/find-duplicate-ids.mjs). Add a `contributor` field to the CheckDef schema at lib/scanner/registry.ts:82 and credit it on the check page, which is what makes a first contribution feel worth the pull request. Then put the live count on the landing page as a growth number rather than a static one: "{N} checks, {M} contributed by people who are not us."

findings.title: Ticketing stops at one one-way GitHub issue holding up to 50 findings, with no per-finding issue, no close-the-loop retest, and no Jira or Linear
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 8: issue tracker integration
findings.description: Jira is universal across all eight commercial vendors, Slack near-universal, and the real differentiator is two-way sync: Detectify's Jira integration updates the finding when the ticket is resolved, and Probely/Snyk goes further, marking the Jira issue Done automatically triggers a retest of that finding. Linear appears only at Intruder (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors-commercial.md, "Table stakes" item 2). VulnRadar's entire ticketing surface is POST /api/v3/scan/github-issue (app/api/v3/scan/github-issue/route.ts:11), which files one issue per scan into one repo, listing at most 50 findings in the body (`MAX_FINDINGS_LISTED = 50`, :26). It is one-way and one-shot: nothing reads the issue's state back, nothing closes it when a rescan shows the finding gone, and there is no per-finding issue so no finding has its own trackable ticket. Notification delivery is limited to Discord, Slack and generic webhooks (lib/webhooks/detect-type.ts:7 to :14) plus email; there is no Jira, Linear, ServiceNow or Teams destination anywhere in lib/.
findings.impact: For the developer this product targets, a single 50-item issue is a dump, not a workflow: it cannot be assigned, prioritised, or closed piecemeal, and once one finding is fixed the issue is stale but still open. For the small security team, the absence of any close-the-loop mechanism means the remediation state lives only inside VulnRadar (lib/scanner/remediation-store.ts) and inside the tracker separately, and the two drift.
findings.recommendation: Do not start with Jira. The GitHub connection already exists, is already authorised for issue writes (lib/github/github-connections.ts), and the finding IDs are already stable across runs (lib/scanner/_helpers.ts generateId, `<checkId>--<urlHash>`), which is exactly what a close-the-loop integration needs and what Jira would still need built. Extend app/api/v3/scan/github-issue/route.ts with a per-finding mode: one issue per finding, titled with the check id, labelled by severity, and stamped with the stable finding id in the body. Then in lib/scanner/regression-alert.ts, which already diffs a completed scan against the previous scan of the same URL by that same id, close any tracked issue whose finding is absent from the new scan and post a one-line comment saying which scan proved it fixed. That is the Probely/Snyk retest loop, built on machinery that already exists. Add Jira only if a paying user asks for it by name.

findings.title: SARIF export and the six-framework compliance crosswalk are shipped, complete, and free on every tier, and neither is mentioned anywhere on the landing page or in any /alternatives comparison row
findings.category: list (b): the strongest shipped feature nobody is told about
findings.description: Two features exist in full and are invisible in marketing. (1) SARIF 2.1.0 export: lib/reports/sarif-report.ts:1 to :253, wired into both the client export menu (components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx:556) and the API (app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts:174). (2) A compliance crosswalk mapping findings to PCI DSS 4.0, SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, OWASP ASVS 4.0, HIPAA and GDPR, built on a documented OWASP-Top-10 backbone with an explicit "Unmapped findings" honesty section rather than force-fitting (lib/reports/compliance-mappings.ts:1 to :80, rendered by lib/reports/compliance-report.ts). Against the researched set this is genuinely differentiated: Burp Suite DAST has no compliance framework mapping at all, which the research calls a real hole in the strongest-in-class product; Snyk paywalls DAST entirely to the Ignite tier at roughly $1,260/yr per developer; compliance views are otherwise standard only at Intruder, Astra, Snyk and Invicti, all of which are enterprise-priced. Yet the shared VulnRadar answers used by every /alternatives table (lib/seo/alternatives.ts:44 to :51) list only licensing, hosting, pricing, onboarding and engine parity, and the API-and-CI row at :240 says only "REST API, webhooks, and CI-friendly scans on every tier". The landing page never uses the words SARIF, PCI, SOC 2 or ISO 27001: app/landing/page.tsx's FAQ and all eleven components/landing/*.tsx files omit them entirely.
findings.impact: The product ships, at $0, two of the exact artifacts that make an enterprise scanner purchasable, and asks visitors to infer them. "I need a SOC 2 evidence artifact" and "I need findings in the GitHub Security tab" are two of the highest-intent reasons anyone shops for a scanner at all, and neither search term has anywhere to land on this site outside the docs.
findings.recommendation: Add two rows to the shared VR object in lib/seo/alternatives.ts:44: `reports: "SARIF 2.1.0, PDF, Markdown, and a PCI DSS / SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / ASVS / HIPAA / GDPR crosswalk. Free tier included."` and `ci: "SARIF straight into GitHub Code Scanning, plus a GitHub Action and a GitLab template."`, and give every entry a matching `them` value (Burp's honest answer is "no compliance mapping"; Snyk's is "DAST is Ignite tier and above"). On the landing page, replace one of the three items in components/landing/landing-features.tsx's SUPPORTING array (:1 to :14) with "The report an auditor asks for": one sentence on the crosswalk, one on SARIF, linking /docs/reports. Keep the voice concrete, for example "Export the same scan as SARIF for the Security tab or as a PCI DSS and SOC 2 crosswalk for the auditor. Both on the free tier."

findings.title: Authenticated scanning here never stores a credential and the product ships zero telemetry, a privacy posture no SaaS peer can match, and it is stated nowhere outside a source-file comment
findings.description: lib/scanner/auth/types.ts:1 to :10 documents a deliberate design: "There is no stored credential anywhere in this codebase: a caller supplies login material directly in a single scan request, it lives in memory for the length of that one request, and it is never written to a table, a log line, an audit record, or the persisted scan result." The route enforces it (app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:56 to :68: logAction records only the non-secret outcome), and the session object reports counts rather than contents (lib/scanner/auth/scan-session.ts:157 to :172). Every one of the eight commercial vendors stores your target credentials in their SaaS by construction, because all of them offer saved recorded login sequences. Separately, components/landing/landing-open-source.tsx:6 to :13 already lists "Telemetry: None" and "Third-party trackers: None" as bare facts in a definition list. The privacy argument is never made anywhere: neither claim appears in any /alternatives comparison row (lib/seo/alternatives.ts:44 has no privacy or data-handling row), in any landing FAQ answer (app/landing/page.tsx), or on the pricing page.
findings.impact: "Do I have to give a third-party SaaS a working login to my staging environment" is the objection that kills authenticated-scanning trials, and it is the one objection this product has an unusually good answer to. Burying that answer in a TypeScript file comment means it never reaches the person deciding.
findings.recommendation: Add a `privacy` row to the shared VR object in lib/seo/alternatives.ts:44: "Login material is sent in one request and held in memory for that request only. Never stored, logged, or written to a scan result." and give each competitor an accurate neutral `them` ("Saved login sequences, stored vendor-side"). Add it to the authenticated-scanning UI as a one-line reassurance above the credential fields, and to app/docs/ wherever authenticated scanning is documented. Pair it with the two existing facts from components/landing/landing-open-source.tsx:10 to :11 into a short "What we never keep" block on the landing page, which is a genuinely different section shape from the icon grids CLAUDE.md's design rules ban.

findings.title: Active probing is nine reflection-and-error-based probes with no out-of-band channel, so blind injection, stored XSS and second-order flaws are structurally undetectable and the marketing should say so
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 11: depth of active testing
findings.description: The research called active injection testing the defining line and ranked it gap number one. Verified in code, VulnRadar is further along than that implies but structurally capped. lib/scanner/active-probe-catalog.ts:46 to :101 defines nine opt-in probes, gated behind verified domain ownership (:117): reflected XSS canary, error-based SQLi, SSTI, OS command injection, confirmed open redirect, GraphQL introspection, active CORS reflection, dangerous HTTP methods, and X-Forwarded-Host injection, implemented in lib/scanner/active-probes/ (five modules, roughly 700 lines). Every one of them decides from the immediate response body or status. There is no out-of-band interaction server anywhere in the repo (grep for oast, collaborator, interactsh across lib/scanner/ returns only unrelated matches in port-scan.ts and two checks-data JSON files), which means blind and time-based SQLi, blind SSRF, blind XXE, out-of-band command injection and Log4Shell-class flaws cannot be confirmed by construction. There is also no second request-cycle verification, so stored XSS is out of reach. By contrast ZAP and Wapiti send full active-scan payloads across 30+ module families including XXE, path traversal, file upload and CSRF, Nuclei adds fuzzing with -dast, Burp ships OAST via Collaborator, Pentest-Tools ships actual auto-exploiters, and Invicti claims runtime proof-based verification at 99.98%.
findings.impact: Two-sided. Against ZAP and Wapiti, VulnRadar genuinely finds less, and a security engineer who assumes "active probing" means ZAP-equivalent coverage will conclude the scanner missed things it never claimed to look for. Against the free graders (Observatory, SecurityHeaders, SSL Labs), VulnRadar finds far more, which is the comparison that actually matters for its funnel. The cost today is not missed findings so much as an unstated ceiling.
findings.recommendation: Do not build an OAST server. It needs a public wildcard DNS zone plus an always-on HTTP collector, it breaks in every self-hosted deployment (which is the differentiator in comp-01), and it is the single most expensive item on this list. If out-of-band detection is ever wanted, integrate the public interactsh server as an optional, off-by-default setting rather than operating one. What is worth doing now is cheap and honest: state the ceiling. Add one line to the active-probes description surface (lib/scanner/active-probe-catalog.ts:44's rendered panel and app/checks/category/active-probes) saying these probes confirm what the response itself proves and do not attempt blind or time-based detection, and add an /alternatives entry for OWASP ZAP that says plainly that ZAP sends deeper payloads while VulnRadar is the hosted, zero-setup, public-catalog path. Being the tool that documents its own limits is a positioning asset for a scanner whose core pitch is determinism.

findings.title: One free scan already covers headers plus TLS plus DNS and email plus cookies at exactly the moment every free peer narrowed, and the hero copy actively undersells it to headers-only
findings.description: The free grading market contracted sharply and in one direction. MDN HTTP Observatory runs ten tests on HTTP headers only and sunset its TLS/SSH Observatory in October 2024. SecurityHeaders.com covers response headers only and its API was shut down by Snyk in April 2026 (confirmed live this session). SSL Labs covers TLS only, its v4 API rejects free email providers, and commercial use is prohibited by default. Hardenize went enterprise-only under Red Sift. ImmuniWeb is the only broad free option left and caps its free API at eight tests a day. VulnRadar covers all of it in one call: 18 check categories including headers, ssl, tls, dns, email, cookies, configuration, information-disclosure, api, code, secrets-extended, client-side, supply-chain and reputation (lib/scanner/registry.ts:23 to :40), plus port scanning (lib/scanner/port-scan.ts), software inventory with OSV/CVE correlation (lib/scanner/software-inventory.ts, osv-check.ts, cve-enrichment.ts), subdomain discovery, and a self-computed SSL-Labs-style letter grade that depends on no third-party API (lib/scanner/ssl-grade.ts:1). The landing hero shows a six-row readout of security headers and nothing else, and its caption at components/landing/landing-hero.tsx:132 to :136 says "Every header, cookie, and config gets read the same way: no rendering, no screenshot, just the response", which describes a headers scanner and is also inaccurate, since the product does take page screenshots (lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts) and does render pages in a real browser for authenticated login (lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts). Relatedly, components/landing/landing-features.tsx:4 claims "no browser extension" while extension/ ships one to the Chrome store.
findings.impact: The single strongest, most defensible, most timely claim available to this product, that it is now the only free tool covering headers and TLS and DNS together, is not made anywhere, and the hero actively frames the product as the narrower category the incumbents just abandoned. Visitors arriving from a "security headers" search have no reason to learn the scan also graded their certificate and checked their SPF and DMARC records.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the hero caption at components/landing/landing-hero.tsx:132 to name the breadth, for example: "One request, one report: headers, certificate and TLS, cookies, DNS and mail records, exposed secrets. Observatory dropped TLS in 2024 and SSL Labs will not grade a site for you commercially. This does both." Extend HERO_READOUT_ROWS (:25) beyond six header rows to include one TLS row and one DNS or DMARC row so the visual matches the claim. Fix components/landing/landing-features.tsx:4's "no browser extension" to "nothing you have to install" so it stops contradicting the shipped extension. Then add the /alternatives entries from comp-04, since the comparison pages are where this argument converts.

findings.title: Eight signed-in pages use eight different container-plus-padding combinations, including /admin at max-w-7xl which the spec reserves for the footer
findings.description: design-language.md C2 records `max-w-6xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6` as the default (33 uses) and max-w-7xl as footer-only. The signed-in pages disagree eight ways. app/history/page.tsx:443, app/assets/page.tsx, app/repos/page.tsx, app/teams/page.tsx and app/shares/page.tsx use `max-w-6xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6 py-6 sm:py-8`, which is the largest cluster. app/attack-surface/page.tsx:27 uses the same width with `px-4 py-8 sm:px-6` (no sm py step). app/dashboard/page.tsx:61 declares its own `const CONTAINER = "w-full max-w-6xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6"` and applies it with `pb-16` and no top padding at :882, and components/dashboard/dashboard-skeleton.tsx:6 declares the identical const a second time. app/profile/page.tsx uses `max-w-5xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6 lg:px-8 py-8 sm:py-10`, the only page in the repo with an lg:px step. app/admin/page.tsx uses `max-w-7xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6 py-8`. app/badge/page.tsx:? uses `max-w-5xl ... py-8 sm:py-10`. app/admin/ai-chats/[id]/page.tsx:107 uses `max-w-4xl ... py-8`. app/pricing/page.tsx:77 uses `max-w-3xl ... py-20 sm:py-28`, which is not on the documented rhythm at all (the spec has py-16 sm:py-20 standard and py-16 sm:py-24 for at most two prominent sections). The checkout pages add a ninth, covered in dsn-05.
findings.impact: Page content starts and ends at a different horizontal position on nearly every page, so the app never settles. /admin at max-w-7xl is 128px wider than its siblings, which is why AUDIT-011#docs-04 found the same class of drift in the docs shell. The duplicated CONTAINER const means the dashboard skeleton and the dashboard can drift apart silently.
findings.recommendation: Export one token. Add to lib/ui/animations.ts (or a new lib/ui/layout.ts next to it) `export const PAGE_CONTAINER = "w-full max-w-6xl mx-auto px-4 sm:px-6"` and `export const PAGE_PADDING = "py-6 sm:py-8"`, matching the five-page majority. Apply both to app/history, /assets, /repos, /teams, /shares, /attack-surface, /dashboard (deleting the two CONTAINER consts at app/dashboard/page.tsx:61 and components/dashboard/dashboard-skeleton.tsx:6), /profile (dropping the lone lg:px-8 and widening from max-w-5xl to max-w-6xl so it stops being narrower than every page around it) and /admin (narrowing from max-w-7xl). Leave /badge and /admin/ai-chats/[id] narrower deliberately if the content is single-column, but use max-w-4xl for both rather than one of each. Change app/pricing/page.tsx:77's py-20 sm:py-28 to py-16 sm:py-24.

findings.title: Ninety-five lines of hover and selection CSS with thirteen literal HSL colours and !important have zero consumers anywhere in the repo
findings.description: app/globals.css:483-575 defines five utility classes with a documented purpose: .hover-surface ("Use .hover-surface on any interactive element for consistent hover feedback", :485), .hover-surface-subtle, .scanner-selected, .scanner-selected-hover and .scanner-hover. Grepping app/, components/, lib/, scripts/, cli/ and extension/ for any of the five names returns matches only inside globals.css itself. They are dead. design-language.md A3 item 7 already noted that this block hardcodes hover surfaces as literal HSL with !important; what it did not check is that nothing uses them. The block hardcodes thirteen literal colour values that bypass the token system entirely (hsl(220 10% 88% / 0.95), hsl(220 15% 12%), hsl(220 8% 24% / 0.95), hsl(220 10% 92%), hsl(220 10% 85% / 0.5), hsl(220 8% 28% / 0.5), hsl(220 10% 75% / 0.55), hsl(220 8% 30% / 0.55), hsl(220 10% 70% / 0.7), hsl(220 8% 35% / 0.65), hsl(220 10% 50% / 0.12), hsl(220 8% 70% / 0.1), hsl(220 15% 10%)), six of them with !important, and duplicates each one across a .dark twin. The Radix menu-item rules at :519-537 in the same block DO have consumers (every dropdown and select), so the block is not entirely dead and cannot be deleted wholesale.
findings.impact: Ninety-five lines of CSS ship to every visitor for nothing. More usefully, it is a trap: the comment tells the next developer this is the standard way to do a hover state, so a new component adopts it, gets an !important that overrides its own hover:bg-muted/40, and gets a grey that is not a token and will not track a palette change.
findings.recommendation: Delete the .hover-surface, .hover-surface-subtle, .scanner-selected, .scanner-selected-hover and .scanner-hover rules and their .dark twins (app/globals.css:481-517 and :539-575), leaving the [data-radix-menu-content] rules at :519-537 which are live. Rewrite those surviving rules to use tokens instead of literals: background-color: hsl(var(--accent)); color: hsl(var(--accent-foreground)); which is what --accent (213 18% 81% light / 220 8% 22% dark) exists for, and drop the .dark duplicate since the token already switches. Then the documented hover convention becomes `hover:bg-muted/40` or `hover:bg-accent`, which is what the live components already do.

findings.title: Six CSS variables are defined and never read, and eight Tailwind colour utilities are wired to variables that are never defined, so bg-sidebar silently renders nothing
findings.description: Records design-language.md A3 item 8 as an actionable finding, verified against the current tree. app/globals.css:211-213 defines --surface-1, --surface-2 and --surface-3 for the light theme and :256-258 repeats them for dark. No file in app/, components/ or lib/ reads them, and tailwind.config.mjs does not map them to a utility either, so they are unreachable by any means. Separately, tailwind.config.mjs:64-73 declares a full `sidebar` colour group (DEFAULT, foreground, primary, primary-foreground, accent, accent-foreground, border, ring) resolving to hsl(var(--sidebar-background)) and seven siblings. None of those eight variables is defined anywhere in app/globals.css or any other stylesheet, and no component uses bg-sidebar, text-sidebar-foreground or any of the group. So the utilities exist, autocomplete offers them, and each resolves to hsl() with an empty argument, which is an invalid colour the browser drops.
findings.impact: Six dead declarations in the critical CSS. More costly is the sidebar group: a developer building the next sidebar reaches for bg-sidebar because Tailwind's IntelliSense lists it, gets a transparent element with no error in the console or the build, and has to work out why. The product already has two sidebars (/profile and /admin) that both hand-rolled bg-primary/10 instead, which is what that group was presumably added for.
findings.recommendation: Delete --surface-1, --surface-2 and --surface-3 from both blocks in app/globals.css (:210-213 and :255-258). For the sidebar group, decide once: either delete tailwind.config.mjs:64-73 entirely, or define the eight variables in both :root and .dark and use them in the shared section-nav component proposed in dsn-10. Deleting is the smaller change and matches how the two existing sidebars are actually built; if it stays, the variables must be defined in the same commit so the utilities are never resolvable-but-empty.

findings.title: components/ui/badge.tsx's four untokenised variants are not merely off-palette, they have zero call sites, so removing them is free
findings.description: Extends AUDIT-011#design-03, which filed components/ui/badge.tsx:16-19 as the one primitive that hardcodes Tailwind palette colours (bg-blue-500/10 text-blue-600, bg-green-500/10 text-green-600, bg-amber-500/10 text-amber-600, bg-red-500/10 text-red-600) and does not respond to dark mode. What was not established is whether anything uses them. It does not. Across app/ and components/ there are 102 <Badge> instances in 32 files; the only variant values passed are "outline" (5) and "secondary" (7), with the rest defaulting. There is no variant="info", variant="success", variant="warning" or variant="error" anywhere, and badgeVariants is not called directly outside badge.tsx:35. The 60-odd `variant="info"` and `variant="warning"` matches in app/docs/ belong to DocsCallout and LegalCallout, a different component (see dsn-12). Separately, 14 of the 102 instances pass a className that overrides the variant's colours entirely, for example app/admin/page.tsx:1442's `bg-emerald-500/10 text-emerald-500 border-emerald-500/20`, which is the pattern that would have used variant="success" if it worked in dark mode.
findings.impact: The fix AUDIT-011#design-03 asked for looked like it needed a migration and therefore did not happen. It needs no migration. Meanwhile the dead variants sit in the primitive as the apparent house answer for semantic badges, which is why 14 call sites reached past them for a raw palette className instead.
findings.recommendation: Delete lines 16-19 of components/ui/badge.tsx outright; nothing imports them. Then add one tokenised replacement so the 14 className-override sites have somewhere to go: a `tone` prop taking neutral | primary | success | warning | destructive | severity, resolving to `bg-[hsl(var(--success))]/10 text-[hsl(var(--success-text))] border-[hsl(var(--success))]/25` and siblings using the foreground tokens from dsn-01. Migrate the raw-palette call sites to it: app/admin/page.tsx:1430,1442,1577, components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:666,915,1039,1051, components/admin/features/engine-feedback-manager.tsx:86, components/admin/audit/audit-log.tsx:570,689 and components/profile/tabs/developer/schedules-section.tsx:304 (the last of which is also the only dark: override in the whole app outside the landing page).

findings.title: Three lookup tables paint status with raw Tailwind palette colours instead of the tokens beside them, including one that reimplements the severity scale the product has a single source of truth for
findings.description: design-language.md A2 records that the codebase is genuinely clean of raw Tailwind palette colours; the exceptions it names are components/ui/badge.tsx and the globals.css safelist. Three more exist, all in lookup tables where a token equivalent is already in use one line away. (1) components/badge/badge-types.ts:27-36 returns text-red-500 / text-amber-500 / text-emerald-500 and bg-red-500/10 / bg-amber-500/10 / bg-emerald-500/10 from getSeverityColor and getSeverityBg, a second severity scale beside the single source of truth at components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:37-78; consumed by components/badge/badge-scan-list.tsx:91,96,101,130. That is tell-tale 9 (severity via SEVERITY_TONE) failing. (2) components/teams/teams-types.ts:62-70 mixes vocabularies inside one table: owner and admin use tokens (--warning, primary), manager uses indigo-500 and operator uses orange-500, member and viewer use --muted. (3) components/shared/stat-icon.tsx:13-14 and its duplicate at components/admin/shared/stat-card.tsx:13-14 carry purple-500 and orange-500 among otherwise tokenised tones. Smaller instances: app/admin/page.tsx:1430,1442,1577 and components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:666,915,1039,1051,1997 use amber-500 and emerald-500; components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx:412 uses purple-500; components/admin/utils.ts:209 uses emerald-500; components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx:309,1349 and components/badge/badge-preview.tsx:114 use emerald-500; app/unsubscribe/page.tsx:288 sets an h1 to text-emerald-500. app/globals.css:9 then safelists eleven of these literal classes with @source inline because the role-badge lookup lives outside Tailwind's content globs.
findings.impact: Since the whole product uses exactly three `dark:` overrides (the theme is entirely token-driven), a raw palette colour is a colour that does not participate in theming at all, and every one of these lands in the light-mode contrast band measured in dsn-01: amber-500 on its own tint is 1.79:1 in light mode, emerald-500 is 2.07:1, orange-500 is 2.27:1. Table (1) also means the /badge page rates a scan on a scale that can drift from the real one, which is precisely what severity-badge.tsx's docblock exists to prevent.
findings.recommendation: (1) Delete getSeverityColor and getSeverityBg from components/badge/badge-types.ts and have components/badge/badge-scan-list.tsx call severityTone() from components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx, mapping its safe/caution/unsafe rating onto info/medium/critical. (2) In components/teams/teams-types.ts change manager to `bg-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]/10 text-[hsl(var(--chart-4))] border-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]/20` only if a fifth hue is genuinely needed; better, drop the per-role hue entirely and distinguish roles by the existing ROLE_ICONS plus a neutral badge, keeping the accent for owner alone. (3) After dsn-06 merges the two tone tables, replace purple-500 and orange-500 in the surviving components/shared/stat-icon.tsx with `bg-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]/10 text-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]` and `--chart-3`, which are the tokens for exactly this job. Then the @source inline safelist at app/globals.css:9 can shrink to whatever the role-badge lookup still needs.

findings.title: Three-across identical card grids in the docs, where the same information is a three-row table on the landing page
findings.description: Tell-tale 5 (no three-across identical cards) has exactly two live instances in app/, both in the docs. app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:89-125 renders `grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3 gap-4` of three <Card> elements, one per webhook platform, each holding a Badge, a one-line description and an InlineCode URL pattern: three items with three parallel attributes, which is a table. app/docs/extension/page.tsx:227-252 renders `grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-3 gap-4` of three <Card> elements for the three auto-scan modes, each a name plus a sentence, which is a definition list. Neither opens with an icon in a rounded square, so they are the mild form of the pattern rather than the full giveaway, and the rest of the docs (60-odd DocsCallouts, DocsTable, DocsSteps, DocsEndpointCard) is a coherent system. The webhooks grid also colours the Discord badge with `bg-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]/10 text-[hsl(var(--chart-4))]` at :96-97, using the chart ramp as a brand colour. app/docs/setup/page.tsx:78 is a third `grid grid-cols-3` but it is three big numerals in a step counter, not cards, and it is fine except for the `font-bold` at :83,94,105.
findings.impact: Two pages out of twenty read as generic where the other eighteen do not, and the webhooks one is the page a developer lands on to answer "does it support Slack", so it is a comparison question answered in a layout that makes comparison hard: the reader has to scan across three cards to line up the three URL patterns.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:89-125 as the semantic table pattern from design-language.md D4 item 3, which the landing page already uses at components/landing/landing-categories.tsx:81: `overflow-x-auto rounded-xl border border-border/60` wrapping `w-full text-sm border-collapse` with a sr-only caption, columns Platform / URL pattern / Payload shape, `<th scope="row">` on the platform name, thead at `border-b border-border/60 bg-muted/30`. Drop the chart-ramp brand colour on the Discord badge; if one row deserves an accent it is Generic, since that is the one most readers need. Rewrite app/docs/extension/page.tsx:227-252 as the divided definition list from D4 item 1: `divide-y divide-border/50 border-y border-border/50` with each mode as a `py-4` row, `<dt className="text-sm font-semibold text-foreground">` and `<dd className="mt-1 text-sm text-muted-foreground leading-relaxed">`. Change the three font-bold numerals at app/docs/setup/page.tsx:83,94,105 to font-semibold.

findings.title: The pricing table lifts and shadows its highlighted plan, the only hover-lift-and-shadow treatment in the product
findings.description: components/pricing/pricing-cards.tsx:72 gives the popular plan `border-primary bg-card shadow-lg shadow-primary/10 lg:-translate-y-1.5` while its three siblings get `border-border/50 bg-card/50`. design-language.md D1 records that shadows in this system are near-invisible (shadow-xs on the shadcn Card, `shadow-xs shadow-black/5` on the hero readout) and tell-tale 10 names `hover:shadow-xl hover:-translate-y-1` as the fail case. This is the static version of it: a coloured glow plus a 6px lift, and it is the only elevated-and-offset card in app/ or components/ outside a modal. The card is already differentiated three other ways (a full-opacity primary border against /50 siblings, a full-opacity bg-card against /50, and an absolutely positioned "Most picked" pill at :77), so the shadow and the lift are the fourth and fifth signals for one fact.
findings.impact: Small, but it is on the page whose entire job is to look trustworthy, and the lift is the single most recognisable marketing-template gesture in web design. Anyone who has seen a SaaS pricing page recognises it immediately, which undercuts the honest-and-specific positioning the landing page spends nine sections building.
findings.recommendation: Change components/pricing/pricing-cards.tsx:72 to `border-primary bg-card`, dropping shadow-lg, shadow-primary/10 and lg:-translate-y-1.5. The border-versus-border/50 and bg-card-versus-bg-card/50 contrast plus the pill at :77 already carry it, and it matches how the landing page marks its one flagship table row (components/landing/landing-categories.tsx, `border-primary/25 bg-primary/5`, no shadow, no offset). If more emphasis is wanted, add `bg-primary/5` to the popular card rather than elevation.

findings.title: The email wordmark is set in bold sans-serif, while the VulnRadar wordmark is monospace on every other surface
findings.description: The email lockup at lib/email/email.ts:151-156 renders the logo image next to `VulnRadar` with no font-family, so it inherits the body's sans stack from :145. Everywhere else the wordmark is monospace: components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:67 and the footer at :35 (recorded in audits/AUDIT-011/design-language.md B1, "mono is load-bearing brand, not just code"), app/not-found.tsx:27 `text-xl font-mono font-semibold`, app/error.tsx:42 the same, public/og-image.svg, and all five extension store PNGs. The weight is also off the scale: design-language B3 records three weights only (default, font-medium, font-semibold) and that font-bold appears nowhere in the strong work, while the email uses 700 here and again in emailHeading at :194. The logo image also carries `alt=""` (:153), which is defensible because the wordmark text sits beside it, but combined with the fact that most clients block images by default it means the first thing a recipient sees is the sans wordmark alone.
findings.impact: Email is the surface seen furthest from the product, in a list beside every other sender, and the one visual cue meant to identify VulnRadar at a glance is set in the same generic system sans as everything else in the inbox. The mono wordmark is the strongest single piece of brand equity the product has and it is absent from the only place a stranger sees the brand cold.
findings.recommendation: In lib/email/email.ts:154, add `font-family: 'SFMono-Regular', ui-monospace, Menlo, Consolas, monospace;` to the wordmark span and drop the weight to 600, matching not-found.tsx:27. Keep letter-spacing at 0 rather than -0.2px, since mono does not need the optical tightening a sans wordmark does. Drop emailHeading's weight at :194 from 700 to 600 as well so the two-weight rule holds across the email set. The same monospace declaration already exists three times in the file (:226, :260, :299), so lift it to a `const MONO_STACK` at the top of the module and use it in all four places.

findings.title: The Chrome Web Store screenshots advertise 700+ checks against a real registry count of 795+, and there is no source file that could regenerate them
findings.description: store_1.png's monospace footnote reads "700+ checks across headers, TLS, DNS, email auth, secrets, and client-side code" (transcribed from the PNG, and independently recorded in audits/AUDIT-011/design-language.md E3). The real figure is lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts:8, `GENERATED_CHECKS_LABEL = "795+"`, which flows through CONFIG_TOTAL_CHECKS_LABEL (lib/config/config-values.ts:133) into TOTAL_CHECKS_LABEL and is regenerated on every build by the knowledge-compile prebuild scripts. The five store PNGs are committed binaries with no source: extension/scripts/ holds only build.mjs, generate-icons.mjs, package.mjs and package-source.mjs, none of which reference store_*, and there is no .svg, .html or design file for them anywhere in the repo. So the one number in the marketing art has drifted 95 checks below the product and there is no mechanism to correct it short of rebuilding the art by hand. Design-language rule 8 requires numbers to be real and pulled from the registry at render time; a baked PNG cannot honour that, which is precisely why it needs a source. Merged from mkt-12, filed independently from the marketing surface. No source file exists that could regenerate the five store PNGs, so the correction is a manual re-export.
findings.impact: The store listing undersells the scanner by roughly 12 percent to every prospective installer, and the number will keep drifting further with every new check family added. Because the art is unreproducible, correcting it is a design project rather than a one-line change, so in practice it will not be corrected and the gap will widen.
findings.recommendation: Add the missing source. Create extension/store/store-1.html through store-5.html as 1600x1000 HTML pages using the same generated token file from dsnx-03, reproducing the composition the PNGs already establish and that design-language E3 documents: alternating copy side (left on 1, 3, 5; product left on 2 and 4), the mono wordmark lockup top-left, a two-tone headline with the second clause in #60a5fa, a muted body paragraph, and a monospace footnote with a bold lead clause. Inject the check count from lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts at render time so it can never drift again. Add extension/scripts/build-store-shots.mjs that renders each to PNG (the repo already depends on sharp, used by scripts/build-og-image.mjs, and the same Playwright-free approach used there works if the pages are authored as SVG instead of HTML). Keep it a manual script like build-og-image.mjs rather than a build hook, but have it fail if the baked number differs from the current label.

findings.title: The CSV export writes no UTF-8 BOM, so Excel on Windows mojibakes the same arrows the PDF garbles
findings.description: exportCsv (components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx:224-252) joins the rows and builds `new Blob([csv], { type: "text/csv;charset=utf-8;" })` at :250 with no byte order mark. The charset parameter on a Blob MIME type is not written into the file and has no effect on what a spreadsheet application infers when the file is opened from disk. Excel on Windows defaults a .csv with no BOM to the system ANSI code page, so the same 96 non-ASCII characters catalogued in dsnx-01 come back as mojibake: the fixSteps column carries U+2192 in over ten secrets-extended.json entries and is exported at :244 as `f.fixSteps.join(" | ")`, and the description column carries U+00A7 from email.json. The Markdown, SARIF and JSON exports are unaffected because their consumers all assume UTF-8.
findings.impact: CSV is the export a non-engineer picks, and the column it damages is the remediation instructions. A security lead who pulls the findings into a spreadsheet to assign work distributes rows reading "Revoke the token immediately via GitHub Settings â†' Developer Settings".
findings.recommendation: Prefix the BOM at components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx:250: `new Blob(["\uFEFF", csv], { type: "text/csv;charset=utf-8;" })`. Apply the same change to the other CSV writer in the repo, app/api/v3/admin/audit-log/export/route.ts, and to components/compare/compare-actions-menu.tsx if it builds one. Better, move the blob construction into lib/ui/download.ts as `downloadCsv(rows, filename)` next to the existing escapeCsv helper (lib/ui/download.ts:23) so the BOM is applied once and every future CSV inherits it. While there, add the four summary lines the PDF and Markdown reports carry (url, scanned at, safety rating, severity counts) as a commented preamble or a second sheet-style header block, since the CSV is currently the only export with no scan context at all.

findings.title: The compliance crosswalk is the one report with no rendered form: it exports as raw Markdown to the audience least likely to read Markdown
