findings.title: The password strength gate `score < 3` is repeated as an unnamed literal in five routes and one component with no shared constant and no way to tune it
findings.description: analyzePassword returns a 0-4 style score (lib/auth/password-strength.ts:417). The cutoff that decides whether a password is accepted is written as the bare comparison `pwAnalysis.score < 3` in four server routes: app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:89, app/api/v3/auth/reset-password/route.ts:47, app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:302 and app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts:171. components/auth/reset-password-form.tsx:49 repeats `analysis.score < 3` client-side to drive the advisory meter. There is no exported constant and no registry key; a grep of lib/config for a password-score setting returns only PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH. The comment at lib/auth/password-strength.ts:663 explicitly notes the score is 'useful for a strength meter, useless as' a gate on its own, yet five sites gate on it.
findings.impact: Raising or lowering the strength bar means finding and editing five identical comparisons, and missing the client one leaves the meter green on a password the server will reject. The gate is also invisible to an operator: nothing in the admin panel or the docs states that a password can fail after passing the documented length check.
findings.recommendation: Export a MIN_PASSWORD_SCORE constant from lib/auth/password-strength.ts, use it at all five sites, and document it next to PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH in app/docs/account-security so users understand why a 12-character password can still be refused.

findings.title: The scan-tag input accepts 50 characters and tells the user so, while the server truncates at the admin-configurable MAX_TAG_LENGTH of 30 with no feedback
findings.description: components/history/scan-tags.tsx:15 sets MAX_CLIENT_TAG_LENGTH = 50, used for the maxLength attribute at :165 and for the error copy at :73, `Keep tags under ${MAX_CLIENT_TAG_LENGTH} characters.` The server does not reject an overlong tag: app/api/v3/scan/tags/route.ts:70-:71 reads getSetting('MAX_TAG_LENGTH') and silently truncates with `tag.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, maxTagLength)`. The default is 30 (lib/config/config-values.ts:1039, admin-editable at lib/config/registry.ts:2705). The component's own doc comment at :8-:14 acknowledges the split, explaining that 50 is the VARCHAR(50) column guard rather than the enforced limit, so the divergence is deliberate; the message shown to the user is not.
findings.impact: A tag between 31 and 50 characters is accepted by the form, sent, silently shortened, and comes back as a different string than the user typed, with the error copy having just promised them 50 characters were fine. On a deployment that lowered MAX_TAG_LENGTH further, the gap widens with no UI change.
findings.recommendation: Expose MAX_TAG_LENGTH through the existing client config endpoint (app/api/v3/config/client/route.ts already carries FEATURE_PDF_REPORTS), use it for both maxLength and the error copy, and keep 50 only as the hard column guard it is documented to be.

findings.title: The auth SWR cache window is a bare 300000 literal that two other files describe as '5 minutes' in prose
findings.description: components/providers/auth-provider.tsx:90 sets `dedupingInterval: 300000` with no named constant. Three comments elsewhere restate that number in words and build reasoning on it: the same file at :153 ('dedupingInterval (5 minutes)'), app/profile/page.tsx:508-:516 (which explains that without a refreshAuthCache() call a saved setting 'stayed invisible to every other page for up to 5 minutes'), and components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx:121-:123 ('a just-canceled plan stays visible elsewhere (paywalls, nav, dashboard) for up to 5 minutes'). A related pair of numbers has the same problem: app/api/v3/config/client/route.ts:36 sends `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60` while lib/config/runtime-config.ts:23 holds the server-side settings snapshot for TTL_MS = 30_000, so a flag change takes up to 90 seconds to reach a browser and neither number references the other.
findings.impact: Halving the deduping interval to make saved settings propagate faster leaves three comments across two other files asserting a window that no longer exists, and those comments are the only record of why refreshAuthCache() must be called at each of those save sites.
findings.recommendation: Name it (AUTH_CACHE_DEDUPE_MS in components/providers/auth-provider.tsx, exported) and have the two profile comments reference the constant rather than restating the number. Add a one-line note at app/api/v3/config/client/route.ts:36 tying its max-age to lib/config/runtime-config.ts's TTL_MS so the combined propagation delay is visible in one place.

findings.title: A tunables comment in config-values.ts states CONFIG_BROWSERBASE_MAX_TTL_SECONDS = 300 five lines above the line that sets it to 360
findings.description: lib/config/config-values.ts:907-:909 reads 'Tunables: CONFIG_BROWSERBASE_MAX_TTL_SECONDS = 300 (5 min hard cap, matches the product promise and prevents runaway sessions).' Line 913 sets `export const CONFIG_BROWSERBASE_MAX_TTL_SECONDS = 360;` and the immediately preceding comment at :911-:912 explains the 360 as 'a 60-second buffer over the 5-minute user budget'. So the file states two different values for the same constant within six lines, and the stale one is in the block an operator reads first. This is the in-file twin of AUDIT-011#drift-31, which found the published API docs stating a browser-session TTL default 60 seconds below the real value; that finding covered app/docs/api/page.tsx:525, not this comment.
findings.impact: An operator scanning the configuration file for the session cap reads 300, sizes their Browserbase minute budget on it, and is billed against 360. It also makes the AUDIT-011#drift-31 docs fix look already done when the source of the wrong number is still in the tree.
findings.recommendation: Update the Tunables block at lib/config/config-values.ts:908 to 360 and fold in the buffer explanation that already sits at :911, so there is one statement of the value in the file.

findings.title: The same five-step checkout retry ladder is copy-pasted into four billing components, giving an unnamed and unadjustable 8-second webhook confirmation budget
findings.description: `const delays = [500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000];` appears verbatim in components/billing/stripe-checkout.tsx:66, components/billing/ai-credit-checkout.tsx:77, components/billing/browserbase-credit-checkout.tsx:72 and components/billing/github-credit-checkout.tsx:71, each followed by the same `for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= delays.length; attempt++)` loop that polls the confirm endpoint six times and then falls through to a 'pending' state. Total wall-clock budget is 8 seconds. Nothing names the array, nothing explains why five steps, and there is no constant tying the budget to how long the Stripe webhook typically takes to land.
findings.impact: If Stripe's webhook is slower than 8 seconds, all four purchase flows show a pending state to a user who has just been charged, and a maintainer widening the window has to find and edit four identical arrays. A partial edit leaves the credit purchases and the subscription purchase behaving differently for the same underlying delay.
findings.recommendation: Extract the ladder to one exported constant (CHECKOUT_CONFIRM_BACKOFF_MS in a shared billing module) and import it in all four components, with a comment recording the total budget so the next person changing it knows what they are trading against.

findings.title: Six user-facing list endpoints carry hard SQL LIMITs with no pagination, no total, and no client-side awareness of the cap
findings.description: AUDIT-013#dup-15 verified that the seven properly paginated routes share one page/limit convention. These six do not participate in it and cap silently instead: app/api/v3/support-tickets/route.ts:45 (LIMIT 100 on a user's own tickets), app/api/v3/admin/support-tickets/route.ts:56 (LIMIT 200 on the staff inbox), app/api/v3/scan/remediation/route.ts:165 (LIMIT 500 on triage state), app/api/v3/teams/member-scans/route.ts:58 (LIMIT 50), app/api/v3/badge/scans/route.ts:34 (LIMIT 50) and app/api/v3/admin/blocked-data/route.ts:80 (LIMIT 100). None returns a total. Two of them then feed a client-side paginator that reports the capped array as the total: components/teams/team-member-scans.tsx:124 passes totalItems={scans.length} over the server-capped 50, and components/ui/pagination-control.tsx:11 offers page sizes of 10, 25, 50 and 100, so selecting 100 on the teammate-scans panel yields a single page that can never contain more than 50 rows. A related client blind spot: app/api/v3/scan/remediation/bulk/route.ts:31 caps the items array at 200 via zod, but components/scanner/results-list.tsx:176 sends `[...selected]` unchunked and its catch at :219-:221 sets a generic bulkError flag, so an over-cap submission fails with no explanation of the limit.
findings.impact: A long-running account's support history, triage state and teammate activity are truncated with no indication, and the paginator actively asserts the truncated count is the total. On the staff inbox the 200-row cap means an older open ticket can drop off the only list staff have.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the page/limit convention AUDIT-013#dup-15 documented for these six routes, returning a total alongside the rows, and pass that total into PaginationControl instead of array length. For the bulk remediation cap, export the 200 as a shared constant and have components/scanner/results-list.tsx chunk at it rather than relying on a server rejection.

findings.title: Two more product-surface tablists declare tab roles with no tabpanel, aria-controls or arrow-key navigation
findings.description: Extends AUDIT-011#docs-11, which covered components/docs/docs-code-tabs.tsx:30 and app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:420. The same incomplete pattern exists twice more, outside docs: components/scanner/issue-detail.tsx:896-916 renders `role="tablist" aria-label="Code examples"` with `role="tab" aria-selected` buttons over a `<CodeBlock>` at :921 that is not `role="tabpanel"` and carries no id, and no button has `aria-controls`; app/assets/page.tsx:159-183 renders the My-scans / All-public-hosts scope toggle as `role="tablist"` + `role="tab" aria-selected` where the thing it switches is the page's own list, with no tabpanel, no aria-controls and no roving tabindex. Neither has an onKeyDown for ArrowLeft/ArrowRight, so the arrow-key roving focus the tab role promises is absent in both. Of the five tablists in the repo, only app/docs/api/page.tsx:1235-1263 is complete (aria-controls="code-tabpanel" at :1246 with a matching role="tabpanel" at :1263).
findings.impact: Assistive tech announces "tab, 1 of 3" and then arrow keys do nothing, which is worse than announcing plain buttons because the user is told a navigation model that is not implemented. On issue-detail this is the fix-example switcher inside every finding, so it is on the product's main output path rather than in docs.
findings.recommendation: For app/assets/page.tsx:159, drop the tablist/tab roles entirely and use `aria-pressed` toggle buttons, which is what the control actually is (the codebase already uses that shape 27 times). For components/scanner/issue-detail.tsx:896, either do the same or complete the pattern: give CodeBlock a wrapper with `role="tabpanel" id` and `aria-labelledby`, give each button an id and `aria-controls`, and add ArrowLeft/ArrowRight roving focus.

findings.title: The signed-in app header marks the current page with colour alone, with no aria-current, while the landing nav next to it does it correctly
findings.description: components/scanner/header.tsx:153-183 is the primary navigation for every signed-in page. It computes `const active = isNavActive(href)` at :155 and expresses it only as `bg-primary/10 text-primary font-medium` at :166, with no `aria-current`. The `<nav>` at :153 also has no `aria-label`, and neither does the mobile one at :234, so a screen reader lists two or three unnamed navigation landmarks per page. Thirteen other places in the codebase do set aria-current, including the landing nav that renders in exactly the same slot for signed-out users (components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:82 and :159), the docs sidebar (components/docs/docs-sidebar.tsx:53), the legal nav (components/legal/legal-nav.tsx:43) and the pagination control (components/ui/pagination-control.tsx:171). The admin link at header.tsx:171-181 has the same gap.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user in the signed-in app is never told which nav item corresponds to the page they are on, and the visual cue that would tell a sighted user is a colour that itself fails contrast in light mode (see a11y-02: text-primary on bg-primary/10 computes to 2.08:1). WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color plus a missed 4.1.2 name-role-value.
findings.recommendation: Add `aria-current={active ? "page" : undefined}` to the Link at components/scanner/header.tsx:158 and to the admin Link at :171, matching components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:82. Add `aria-label="Main"` to the nav at :153 and `aria-label="Mobile"` to the one at :234.

findings.title: The shared modal hook never hides the page behind the dialog from assistive tech, despite its own comment claiming it does
findings.description: lib/hooks/use-modal-a11y.ts is the accessibility layer for eleven hand-rolled modals. Its comment at :58-61 says the Tab trap stops a keyboard user stepping out "into the (aria-hidden) page behind it", but nothing in the file ever sets aria-hidden or inert on anything: the three effects handle Escape (:45-56), Tab containment (:62-93) and focus save/restore (:96-118), and `dialogProps` (:121-128) applies only role, aria-modal, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby and tabIndex to the panel itself. The parenthetical describes behaviour that does not exist. Radix's Dialog, which components/ui/dialog.tsx wraps, does apply aria-hidden to sibling nodes, so the hand-rolled modals behave differently from the shadcn ones in the same app.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user in browse mode can still arrow through the whole page behind an open modal, including the ToS gate (components/modals/tos-modal.tsx:164) whose entire purpose is to block interaction until accepted. Real but bounded: aria-modal="true" causes most modern screen readers to constrain the virtual buffer anyway, so this is a belt-and-braces gap rather than an outright block.
findings.recommendation: In lib/hooks/use-modal-a11y.ts, add an effect that sets `inert` (with an aria-hidden fallback) on the direct children of document.body other than the modal's own portal root while `open` is true, and clears it on close. Then correct the comment at :59 either way.

findings.title: The risk-score trend chart has no keyboard access and no text alternative for its data series
findings.description: components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:118-159 renders a recharts AreaChart of up to 30 risk scores for a host. The `<AreaChart>` at :123 does not pass recharts' `accessibilityLayer` prop, so the SVG is not focusable and has no keyboard-driven point navigation; the only way to read a value is `<ChartTooltip>` at :148, which recharts fires on mouse move. There is no `<table>` fallback, no `aria-label` summarising the series, and no `role="img"` with a description. The surrounding text (:91-113) gives only the point count and the delta from oldest to newest, not the series. The product's own accessibility statement pre-declares this at app/legal/accessibility/page.tsx:125-128 ("Complex data visualizations: Some security scan result charts may require additional screen reader descriptions"), which is why this is low rather than medium. Worth contrasting with components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:135-142, where the SeverityDistribution bar does the right thing: `role="img"` plus an aria-label that spells out every count.
findings.impact: A keyboard or screen-reader user on a /host/[hostname] page cannot read any individual score in the trend, only that the chart exists. The gap is disclosed rather than hidden, so it is honest, but it is still a WCAG 1.1.1 failure on the page's headline visual.
findings.recommendation: Add `accessibilityLayer` to the AreaChart at components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:123 (recharts then makes the chart focusable and moves a keyboard cursor through points with arrow keys), and add an sr-only `<table>` or an aria-label built from `toChartData(points)` listing each date and score, mirroring the aria-label approach in components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:137.

findings.title: Seven admin row-action buttons are rendered at opacity-0 with only a hover trigger, so keyboard focus lands on invisible controls
findings.description: These row-action controls use `opacity-0 group-hover:opacity-100` with no focus variant: components/admin/teams/teams-list.tsx:483, :496, :514; components/admin/features/ip-rules-manager.tsx:804, :819; components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:1834; components/admin/audit/audit-log.tsx:462. `opacity-0` does not remove an element from the tab order, so the buttons stay focusable while remaining invisible, and the global focus ring at app/globals.css:370 is painted on a fully transparent element. Twenty-seven other hover-reveal sites in the same admin panel already pair the hover trigger with `group-focus-within:opacity-100` or `focus-visible:opacity-100` (for example components/admin/features/security-alerts-manager.tsx:367, components/admin/notifications/notifications-manager.tsx:625, app/admin/page.tsx:1463), so the fix pattern is established and these seven were just missed.
findings.impact: A staff member tabbing through a team or IP-rule list hits stops where nothing is visible, including a delete action at teams-list.tsx:514, with no indication of what is focused or what Enter would do. WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.7. Admin-only, so low.
findings.recommendation: Append `group-focus-within:opacity-100 focus-visible:opacity-100` to each of the seven className strings, matching components/admin/features/security-alerts-manager.tsx:367.

findings.title: The competitor comparison table has no scope on its header cells and no caption
findings.description: app/alternatives/[competitor]/page.tsx:110-130 renders a three-column comparison table whose `<th>` elements at :113, :116, :119 (column headers) and :127 (a row header per feature) carry no `scope` attribute, and the table has no `<caption>`. Every other table in the repo does this correctly: components/docs/docs-table.tsx uses `scope="col"` / `scope="row"` and an sr-only `<caption>` in all four of its variants (:62, :111, :114-136, :184, :239), components/landing/landing-categories.tsx:83 and components/pricing/pricing-features.tsx:193 both have sr-only captions. This one page is the outlier, and it is a generated SEO route so the markup repeats once per competitor.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user navigating the comparison grid cell by cell is not told which column or feature row each cell belongs to, so a table whose whole purpose is a per-row VulnRadar-versus-competitor comparison reads as a flat list of Yes/No values. WCAG 1.3.1.
findings.recommendation: Add `scope="col"` to app/alternatives/[competitor]/page.tsx:113, :116, :119 and `scope="row"` to :127, plus an sr-only `<caption>` naming the comparison, copying components/docs/docs-table.tsx:111-114.

findings.title: Markdown H1s in AI chat replies inject additional h1 elements into whatever page the widget is open on
findings.description: components/ai-chat/message-content.tsx:24 and the duplicate map in components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx:207 render a markdown `#` heading as `<h1 className="text-sm font-semibold mt-3 mb-1.5 first:mt-0" {...props} />`. The ChatWidget is mounted globally from app/layout.tsx:190, so an assistant reply containing a top-level markdown heading emits a second (or third) `<h1>` into the current page's heading tree, at a font size of 14px and nested inside a `role="dialog"`. The model's output is not constrained here, and the docs knowledge files it draws from are markdown with `#` headings.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user navigating by heading level on, say, /dashboard finds extra top-level headings that belong to a chat message rather than the page, and the document outline no longer matches the visual hierarchy. Bounded: it only occurs while the widget is open and only for replies that use a top-level heading.
findings.recommendation:
Demote the mapping in both files: render markdown `#` as `

` (or `

`) inside the chat transcript, and shift h2/h3 down accordingly, so nothing inside the widget competes with the page's own h1.

findings.title: Input and card borders sit at 1.21:1 to 1.54:1 against their own surfaces, below the 3:1 non-text minimum
findings.description: app/globals.css:194-195 sets light `--border`/`--input: 213 16% 78%` against `--background: 213 25% 90%` (:172) and `--card: 213 22% 95%` (:174), and :240-241 sets dark `--border`/`--input: 224 15% 16%` against `--background: 224 20% 6%` (:224) and `--card: 224 18% 9%` (:226). Computed: light border vs background 1.36:1 and vs card 1.54:1; dark border vs background 1.28:1 and vs card 1.21:1. components/ui/input.tsx:11 gives every field `border border-input bg-background` and no other visual boundary, so the border is the sole indicator of where the control is. WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast requires 3:1 for the visual boundary of a UI component when that boundary is what identifies it.
findings.impact: On a card, an unfilled text field is nearly indistinguishable from the surface it sits on for a low-vision user, in both themes. Low because a filled field's own text and the layout still convey where to type, and because the fields are labelled.
findings.recommendation: Split --border from --input in app/globals.css and darken/lighten only --input to clear 3:1 against both --background and --card in each theme (light around `213 16% 55%`, dark around `224 12% 38%`), leaving --border for decorative dividers where 3:1 is not required.

findings.title: Adding or removing a scan tag no-ops on failure in both the history and dashboard copies: no error, no revert, no indication the click was received
findings.description: app/history/page.tsx:305-319 (`handleAddTag`) and :321-331 (`handleRemoveTag`) POST to API.SCAN_TAGS and do all their work inside `if (res.ok)`. There is no else, no catch at all (an unhandled rejection on a dropped connection), and no error state. app/dashboard/page.tsx:389-400 and :402-412 are the same two functions copied verbatim with the same omission. The tag input at components/history/scan-tags.tsx clears on submit regardless, so the typed tag disappears and never appears in the list. Removing a tag on a failed request leaves the chip in place with no explanation. These are the two handlers AUDIT-011#form-01 did not cover on this page (it named handleSaveNotes at :389 in the pre-refactor numbering).
findings.impact: Tagging is how a user organises scan history, and the failure is completely invisible: the input clears exactly as it does on success, so the user believes the tag was applied and only discovers otherwise when they filter by it later and get nothing. The missing catch also means a network drop produces an unhandled promise rejection rather than any handled path.
findings.recommendation: Wrap all four handlers in try/catch and surface a failure. The history page already has a rendered error slot pattern in its clear-history dialog (`clearError` at :667-669); add an equivalent transient line under the tag row, or reuse the toast used elsewhere on the page. At minimum, do not clear the input in components/history/scan-tags.tsx until the parent's promise resolves, so a failed add leaves the user's text where they can retry it.

findings.title: /repos auto-dismisses its only error banner after 8 seconds while the empty list it explains stays on screen
findings.description: app/repos/page.tsx:142-147 runs `const t = setTimeout(() => setError(null), 8000)` whenever `error` becomes non-null. The error strings it clears are load failures, not transient confirmations: `loadWorkingSet` sets "Failed to load repositories." at :172 and :181 and sets `setRepos([])` alongside it, and the init effect sets "Failed to load your GitHub connection status." at :200. Eight seconds later the banner disappears while the repo list it was explaining is still empty, and nothing in the page then accounts for the emptiness. Separately, `loadSummaries` at :150-160 returns early on `!res.ok` with no error at all, so the per-repo "last scanned" column silently reads as never-scanned.
findings.impact: A user who was reading something else when the page loaded, or who tabs back a few seconds later, sees an empty repository list with no error and no explanation, which reads as "you have no repos selected" rather than "the fetch failed". Auto-dismissal is right for a success toast and wrong for a failure whose cause is still true, and this page has only the one error surface.
findings.recommendation: In app/repos/page.tsx:142-147, keep the auto-dismiss only for transient action errors and make load failures sticky, with a Retry button next to the message that recalls the failed loader. The list's own empty branch should also distinguish "no repos in your working set" from "we could not load them", the way components/repos/repo-detail.tsx:248-255 already does for its own list (once state-04 is fixed).

findings.title: The host risk-score trend chart renders identically for still-loading, fetch-failed and not-applicable, so a broken endpoint is indistinguishable from a chart that has nothing to draw
findings.description: components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:43-59 fetches the trend endpoint, returns early on `!res.ok` at :48 without touching state, and catches at :51-53 with a comment only. `points` therefore stays null in three different situations, and :63's `if (!points) return null` renders nothing for all of them: the request is still in flight, the request failed, or the response was not ok. The file's own docblock at :32-38 documents the design intent and even records that the sub-case of a known host with fewer than two scans was pulled out of this silence precisely because "silence there read as the chart being broken" (:66-82). The same reasoning applies to the failure case, which was left in the silent bucket. The chart also does not reserve its height, so on a slow response it pops in and shifts the panels below it.
findings.impact: On /host/<hostname>, a persistent failure of GET /api/v3/host/<hostname>/trend removes a documented feature with no trace: the user sees the report without the trend and has no reason to think anything is missing. Combined with AUDIT-012#fe-05 (the request cannot start until the host report resolves), a slow trend also produces a late layout shift under content the user is already reading.
findings.recommendation: Split the null: keep `points === null` for in-flight and render a fixed-height skeleton matching the chart's `h-36 sm:h-40` so the layout does not shift, and add a `failed` state set at :48 and :51 that renders one muted line under the existing heading, "Couldn't load the score history.", rather than removing the section. That matches the treatment the same file already gives the fewer-than-two-scans case at :67-82.

findings.title: There is no offline signal anywhere in the app or the extension's web surfaces, so one dropped connection produces a different and mostly wrong message on every screen
findings.description: Grepping `navigator.onLine`, the `online`/`offline` window events and any equivalent across app/, components/, lib/ and extension/src returns only an unrelated staff-status filter string (components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx:71). Nothing in the product knows it is offline. Each surface therefore renders whatever its own catch does for a network failure, and those disagree: /history renders the "No scans recorded yet" empty state (AUDIT-011#hist-02, still present at app/history/page.tsx:231-232), the dashboard analytics renders nothing (AUDIT-011#dash-01, components/scanner/dashboard.tsx:229), /admin renders "Access Denied" (state-10), the notification bell renders "All caught up!" (state-11), the profile Developer tab renders "you have no API keys" (state-05), and the scan form is the only one that gets it right, because components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx:96-104 has a dedicated `network` kind with accurate copy. The extension is the one surface with a real connectivity concept, `connectionFailed` from refreshMe (extension/src/popup/popup.ts:1050) rendered as "Failed to connect" by extension/src/popup/components/connect-pill.ts:38-42, though it points the user at Settings, which is the wrong remedy for a network outage.
findings.impact: Losing wifi in a tunnel or on a flaky connection tells the user, depending on which tab they are on, that their scan history was deleted, that they are not an administrator, and that they have no API keys. Each of those is individually filed above; the shared root is that no component can tell a network failure from a server rejection, so each one guesses, and the guesses are wrong in the alarming direction.
findings.recommendation: Add a small `useOnline()` hook in lib/hooks/ backed by navigator.onLine plus the online/offline window events, and a single app-level band rendered from app/layout.tsx that says "You're offline. Nothing here is up to date." Then let list components read it to choose their message: while offline, a failed fetch renders "Can't reach the server" rather than an empty state, everywhere, without each component needing its own classifier. components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx already models the classified-error approach and its `network` entry is the copy to reuse. In the extension, change connect-pill.ts:38-42 so `connectionFailed` offers "Retry" rather than "Settings", since a network failure is not a key problem.

findings.title: "Get Started" is the primary CTA label in the nav and on three pricing surfaces, and it is the one string on the marketing surface that says nothing
findings.description: components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:124 labels the logged-out primary nav button "Get Started". The same string appears at app/pricing/page.tsx:93 (the billing-disabled page's only CTA) and components/pricing/pricing-cards.tsx:170 (the logged-out paid-plan CTA). It is title case where the rest of the page is sentence case, it names no action, and it is the exact label a generated landing page would use. audits/AUDIT-011/design-language.md section F2.4 already records it as the weakest string on the page; this extends that with the two pricing occurrences and with what to put there instead. The full logged-out CTA map above the fold today is: nav "Get Started" to /signup, hero primary "Start scanning free" to /signup, hero secondary "Try the demo" to /demo. Two of three lead to a signup form, and the third leads to a demo that cannot scan the visitor's site (mkt-01). Every other CTA on the page is written properly: "Create a free account", "Try the demo first", "See a full report", "Try it in the playground", "Read the API docs", "Paste a URL and see what comes back".
findings.impact: Minor on its own, but it is the first button a visitor sees and it is inconsistent with a page whose entire argument is specificity. On the billing-disabled self-host page it is also the only CTA, so the whole page ends on the most generic string available.
findings.recommendation: If mkt-01 ships, make the logged-out nav CTA "Scan a URL" pointing at ROUTES.DEMO and leave the ghost "Log in" beside it, so the fastest action is the one in the nav. If it does not, use "Start free" at components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:124. At app/pricing/page.tsx:93 use "Create an account" for the logged-out case, since that page's whole point is that there is nothing to pay for. At components/pricing/pricing-cards.tsx:170 use "Start free, upgrade later", which is accurate: the button goes to /signup rather than to checkout.

findings.title: Five pairs of /checks pages ship an identical H1 and an identical title tag, including two Django debug pages with identical fix steps, so each pair competes with itself for the same query
findings.description: Scanning the raw `title` field of all 749 non-disabled checks in lib/scanner/checks-data/*.json for case-insensitive duplicates gives five pairs, all of which produce two URLs with the same <title>, the same og:title, and the same H1 (app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:196 renders `How to fix: {check.title}`): "Sensitive information in HTML comments" (/checks/sensitive-comments and /checks/html-comment-leaks), "Weak or broken cryptography detected" (/checks/weak-crypto and /checks/insecure-crypto), "document.write() Usage Detected" (/checks/document-write-usage in content.json at low severity and /checks/cs-document-write-usage in client-side.json at high), "eval() Usage Detected" (/checks/eval-usage in code.json and /checks/vibe-eval-usage in vibe-code.json), and "Django debug mode enabled in production" (/checks/django-debug-page in content.json and /checks/django-debug-page-exposure in information-disclosure.json). The Django pair is the closest: both are critical, both have a byte-identical fixSteps array ["Set DEBUG = False in production settings", "Set ALLOWED_HOSTS to your actual domain names", "Configure a proper error logging backend (Sentry, logging module)"], and their riskImpact sentences differ only in wording. Meta descriptions do differ across all five pairs, so this is duplicate titles and headings rather than duplicate documents. These pairs also account for 6 of the 22 pages in the seo-03 title-collision set.
findings.impact: Ten URLs, five queries, and for each query Google picks one page and treats the other as a near-duplicate to filter out of results. "django debug mode enabled in production" is a real search with real volume and the site answers it twice with the same words, which splits any signal either page would otherwise accumulate.
findings.recommendation: Two options per pair. Where both checks are genuinely distinct detectors (the document.write pair genuinely differs: one is a low-severity content scan, the other a high-severity client-side script scan), differentiate the title in the JSON data itself: "document.write() in page scripts (client-side scan)" versus "document.write() in response body (content scan)". Where they are the same finding twice (the Django pair, whose fix steps are byte-identical), pick the canonical URL and have the other's generateMetadata set `alternates: { canonical: `/checks/${primaryId}` }`, which keeps both URLs live for deep links from a scan result while consolidating the ranking signal. pageMetadata (lib/seo/metadata.ts:83) already takes the canonical from `path`, so this needs a new optional `canonicalPath` option on PageSeoOptions.

findings.title: /admin is served noindex on the stated grounds of saving crawl budget, but it is missing from DISALLOWED_PATHS so robots.txt still invites crawlers to fetch it
findings.description: app/admin/layout.tsx:7 sets privatePageMetadata("Admin", "/admin") and its comment says "Keeping it out of the index also saves crawl budget for the public pages that can actually rank." But lib/seo/routes.ts:107 DISALLOWED_PATHS lists /dashboard, /profile, /compare, /history, /assets, /attack-surface, /repos, /shares, /shared/, /host/, /teams, /checkout, /browser/, /badge, /verify-email, /reset-password, /forgot-password and /unsubscribe, and not /admin. app/robots.ts:60 spreads that list, so the published robots.txt permits /admin and /admin/ai-chats/<id>. The meta tag still keeps both out of the index, so this is a crawl-budget gap rather than an exposure: an anonymous fetch of /admin is bounced to /login by middleware.ts:337 and shows nothing.
findings.impact: Crawlers spend fetches on an admin route that redirects, and each redirect lands on /login?redirect=/admin, which is the exact query-parameter duplicate shape the QUERY_DISALLOW rule at app/robots.ts:52 was added to stop after Search Console flagged it. Small, but it is the one hole in an otherwise complete list, and the file's own comment claims the opposite.
findings.recommendation: Add `"/admin",` to DISALLOWED_PATHS in lib/seo/routes.ts:107 next to /dashboard. Prefix matching covers /admin/ai-chats/<id> automatically, the same way /teams covers /teams/join and /checkout covers /checkout/success. While there, add a test that asserts every route whose metadata comes from privatePageMetadata has a matching DISALLOWED_PATHS prefix, which would have caught this and would catch the next one.

findings.title: Every one of the 805 sitemap URLs carries the same lastmod, the build timestamp, so the field is noise on a 749-page set whose source data changes a few entries at a time
findings.description: app/sitemap.ts:13 computes `const lastModified = new Date()` once and assigns it to every entry at line 17. The comment at lines 10-12 explains the choice as avoiding per-entry timestamp noise, which is right about not calling new Date() per row but produces the opposite of the intended effect: because the route is `force-static` (line 7), the value is frozen at build time and every deploy republishes all 805 URLs with a brand-new identical lastmod. Google's documented position is that it uses lastmod only when it is consistently accurate, and that a site claiming every page changed at the same instant is a signal to ignore the field site-wide. The real modification data exists: the 749 check entries come from lib/scanner/checks-data/*.json (file mtime or git log), the 5 alternatives from lib/seo/alternatives.ts, and the docs pages from their own source files.
findings.impact: The sitemap gives Google no usable freshness signal for 805 URLs, so recrawl scheduling falls back to Google's own heuristics, and the one check page that actually changed after a release is refreshed no sooner than the 748 that did not. On a deploy-frequent repo (3.7.2 with a per-change changelog policy) this republishes the entire sitemap as "all changed" several times a week.
findings.recommendation: Derive lastmod from source. Simplest accurate version: in scripts/compile-checks-knowledge.mjs, which already runs on every prebuild, emit a `{ checkId: isoDate }` map from `git log -1 --format=%cI -- <file>` per checks-data JSON file into lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts, and have CHECK_ROUTES in lib/seo/routes.ts:80 carry a per-route lastModified read from it. Do the same for the docs routes once seo-05 derives them from DOCS_PAGES, using each layout.tsx's git commit date. Keep a single build-time fallback for routes with no source mapping.

findings.title: /alternatives/intelliradar is a comparison page that compares nothing: three of its five table rows say "Varies by product." and its summary describes the category rather than the competitor
findings.description: lib/seo/alternatives.ts:55 defines the `intelliradar` entry, one of five in ALTERNATIVES and therefore one of five sitemap entries at priority 0.6 (lib/seo/routes.ts:72). Its `summary` (line 57) is category-level, not product-level: "IntelliRadar is a security scanning tool in the same broad space as VulnRadar: point it at a target and get back a list of findings. Products in this category differ mostly in what they inspect, how they price, and whether you can run them yourself." Its five ComparisonRow entries put "Varies by product." in the competitor column three times (lines 71, 81, 86), "Check the vendor's site; openness varies by product." once, and "See the vendor's current pricing." once. Its `positioning` opens "If you found VulnRadar while searching for IntelliRadar...". The other four entries (detectify, intruder, probely, qualys) all carry real, specific, factual competitor descriptions, so this is a single outlier in an otherwise well-built cluster. The file's own header comment at lines 1-13 sets the rule the entry breaks: "Competitor pricing is NEVER invented" is honoured, but so is every other fact, leaving the page empty.
findings.impact: A page whose entire competitor column is "Varies by product" is a doorway page for a brand name with no content behind it. In a five-page cluster, one page like this pulls down the perceived quality of the other four, which are genuinely good comparison pages that could rank for "detectify alternative" and "probely alternative". It also fails a human reader instantly, so anyone who does land on it bounces.
findings.recommendation: Either fill it or drop it. Filling it means the same treatment as the detectify entry: a specific description of what IntelliRadar actually is, and real values in the five rows. Dropping it means removing the entry from ALTERNATIVES in lib/seo/alternatives.ts:54-104, which automatically removes the sitemap entry (lib/seo/routes.ts:72 derives from getAllAlternatives()) and leaves a clean four-page cluster. Given the comparison-set gap analysis in section 20, the higher-value move is to spend the same effort adding entries for the open-source self-hostable comparisons (OWASP ZAP, Nuclei) and the single-URL free scanners (Mozilla Observatory, Security Headers, SSL Labs), which are the tools this product is genuinely searched against.

findings.title: The PWA manifest is incoherent: start_url is the auth-gated /dashboard, favicon.png is declared 512x512 but is actually 1024x1024, and there is no maskable icon, no id and no screenshots
findings.description: app/manifest.ts:21 sets `start_url: ROUTES.DASHBOARD` ("/dashboard"), a route that requires a session (middleware.ts:332 redirects anonymous requests to /login) and is Disallowed in robots.txt (lib/seo/routes.ts:110). Anyone who installs the PWA while signed out, or after their session expires, launches into a login redirect. Line 28 declares `{ src: "/favicon.png", sizes: "512x512", type: "image/png" }` but the file is 1024x1024 (read from its PNG IHDR, 93.9 KB), so the declared size does not match the asset; Chrome selects icons by the declared value and DevTools reports the mismatch. There is no icon with `purpose: "maskable"`, so Android renders the square PNG letterboxed inside the adaptive-icon mask. There is no `id`, so changing start_url later would be treated as a different app by Chrome. There is no `screenshots` array, so Android shows the minimal install prompt rather than the richer one. Separately, the same 1024x1024 / 94 KB PNG is the apple-touch-icon (app/layout.tsx:66, `apple: "/favicon.png"`) where 180x180 is the used size, so iOS downloads roughly 32 times the pixels it renders.
findings.impact: A user who installs the app gets an icon that looks wrong on Android and a launch that dumps them at a login screen. The apple-touch-icon costs ~94 KB on iOS home-screen add. None of this is visible in search results, but the manifest is part of the installability surface Lighthouse scores and part of what the product looks like when someone takes it seriously enough to install it.
findings.recommendation: In app/manifest.ts: set `start_url: "/"` (middleware.ts:284-288 already routes anonymous to /landing and signed-in to /dashboard, which is exactly the desired behaviour); add `id: "/"`; correct the PNG entry to `sizes: "1024x1024"` or export a real 512x512; add a second entry `{ src: "/icon-maskable.png", sizes: "512x512", type: "image/png", purpose: "maskable" }` with the mark inset to the safe zone; add `screenshots` using the existing 1200x630 card or purpose-shot captures with `form_factor: "wide"` and `"narrow"`. Export a 180x180 apple-touch-icon and point app/layout.tsx:66 at it instead of the 1024px file. The generation can reuse scripts/build-og-image.mjs's sharp pipeline.

findings.title: The indexed check count disagrees across two adjacent marketing surfaces: the landing meta description says "795+ deterministic checks" while the /checks meta description says "the full list of 749 security checks"
findings.description: lib/config/check-stats.generated.ts:8 sets GENERATED_CHECKS_LABEL to "795+", derived from EXACT_CHECK_COUNT = 797 (line 6), which is EXACT_LEGACY_CHECK_COUNT 754 plus EXACT_PAGE_CHECK_COUNT 43. app/landing/page.tsx:32 uses that label verbatim in the landing meta description: "795+ deterministic checks across headers, TLS, cookies, DNS, and secrets". app/checks/page.tsx:26 computes `TOTAL = getAllChecks().length`, which is 754 minus the 5 entries filtered as "(disabled duplicate)" at lib/seo/checks-content.ts:129, giving 749, and line 29 puts that in the /checks meta description: "The full list of 749 security checks VulnRadar runs against a URL". Both numbers are internally defensible (795 counts the 43 PageCheck-architecture detectors that deliberately have no public page, per the comment at lib/seo/checks-content.ts:12-14) and neither is a lie, but they appear in two indexed snippets one click apart and differ by 46.
findings.impact: A visitor who clicks a result promising 795+ checks lands on a page whose own first sentence says 749, which reads as a marketing exaggeration caught in the act. On a product whose entire pitch is deterministic, auditable detection, an unexplained number mismatch on the two highest-traffic public pages is a credibility cost out of proportion to the size of the bug.
findings.recommendation: Make /checks state both numbers so they reconcile rather than contradict. Change app/checks/page.tsx:29 to something like `The ${TOTAL} security checks with a public fix guide, out of ${TOTAL_CHECKS_LABEL} VulnRadar runs, grouped into 18 categories.` and add one sentence to the page body explaining that the remaining detectors run inside multi-page analysis and have no standalone page. Update the first FAQ answer at app/checks/page.tsx:43, which currently says "documents 749 checks", to the same framing so the FAQPage structured data matches.

findings.title: The OG image build script imports sharp, which is not declared in any package.json and is only present as an optional transitive dependency of next
findings.description: scripts/build-og-image.mjs:11 does `import sharp from "sharp"` and is the only way to regenerate public/og-image.png from public/og-image.svg. sharp appears in neither `dependencies` nor `devDependencies` of the root package.json; it resolves today only because it is an optional dependency of next (package-lock.json:9804 lists `"sharp": "^0.34.3"` under next), and the root `overrides` block pins it to ^0.35.0 without declaring it. Any install with `--omit=optional`, any next major that stops shipping sharp, or a platform where sharp's optional binary does not install, makes the script fail with MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The script's own header comment says it is deliberately not a build hook, so the failure only surfaces when someone next edits the card, which is the moment they least want to debug a toolchain.
findings.impact: The OG image is, per AUDIT-011, one of the three strongest design artifacts the project owns, and the only script that can rebuild it depends on a package nothing declares. A self-hoster or contributor who rebrands by editing og-image.svg hits an install error rather than a rebuilt card. Low blast radius but it is squarely on the path of the seo-02 work, which will want the same sharp pipeline.
findings.recommendation: Add `"sharp": "^0.35.0"` to devDependencies in the root package.json so the existing `overrides` entry has something to override and the script has a declared dependency. Do NOT regenerate package-lock.json on Windows to do it: per this repo's history, a Windows-regenerated lockfile strips the Linux native bindings and breaks CI and deploy. Add the entry and graft the corresponding lock nodes, or make the change on Linux/CI. If seo-02 uses next/og instead (which is bundled with next and needs no new dependency), the script can stay as the one sharp consumer.

findings.title: No twitter:site handle and no search-engine verification tokens are configured, and the Organization sameAs lists no social profile, so X cards are attributed to nobody
findings.description: lib/config/config-values.ts:231 sets CONFIG_SEO_TWITTER_HANDLE to the empty string, and both lib/seo/metadata.ts:120 and app/layout.tsx:88 deliberately omit the `twitter:site` tag rather than emit an empty one (which is the right handling of an unset value). Lines 236-237 set CONFIG_SEO_GOOGLE_VERIFICATION and CONFIG_SEO_BING_VERIFICATION to empty strings, so no ownership meta tag is published either; verification may well be done by DNS instead, which is why this is low and not higher. components/seo/structured-data.tsx:75 builds `sameAs` from SEO_GITHUB_URL, DISCORD_INVITE_URL, CHROME_WEB_STORE_URL and FIREFOX_ADDON_URL: four real, config-derived links and no social profile of any kind.
findings.impact: An X card for any page on the site renders without the "@handle" attribution line, so a card someone reshares carries no route back to an account to follow, and X has no verified entity to associate the domain with. sameAs is what answer engines use to resolve a name to one entity, and the brief flags AI assistants not knowing this product as an existing symptom (the primary cause is the Cloudflare block, see seo-23); a sameAs with no social presence gives them less to work with.
findings.recommendation: If an X account exists, set CONFIG_SEO_TWITTER_HANDLE in lib/config/config-values.ts:231 (with the leading @) and add the profile URL to the sameAs array in components/seo/structured-data.tsx:75 via a new CONFIG_SEO_X_URL, keeping the filter(Boolean) so a fork without one publishes nothing. Add the npm package URL to sameAs once the `vulnradar` name is claimed (see AUDIT-013#subdeps-01), plus the GitHub organisation page. Confirm Search Console and Bing ownership are established by DNS; if they are, add a one-line comment at lines 236-237 saying so, because an empty verification constant reads like an oversight.

findings.title: The homepage URL never serves content: / issues a temporary 307 to /landing for anonymous visitors, and the root layout's fallback canonical points at that same redirecting URL
findings.description: middleware.ts:284-289 redirects an anonymous request for "/" to ROUTES.LANDING with NextResponse.redirect(), which defaults to HTTP 307 (temporary). app/page.tsx:7 does the same with redirect("/landing") for anything that reaches it. So the root URL, the one that gets typed, linked and shared, never returns a 200. Meanwhile app/landing/page.tsx:29 sets canonical /landing and lib/seo/routes.ts:26 puts /landing in the sitemap at priority 1.0, so /landing is the declared homepage. Pulling the other way, app/layout.tsx:59 declares `alternates: { canonical: "/" }` as the site-wide fallback, with the comment "Pages without their own canonical fall back to the site root rather than competing with each other": that fallback names a URL that always redirects. It is latent today because all 71 pages set their own canonical (see seo-22), so nothing currently inherits it, but the next page added without a pageMetadata call will canonicalise to a redirect.
findings.impact: Branded results show vulnradar.dev/landing rather than vulnradar.dev, which reads as less authoritative for the site's own name. A temporary redirect also tells Google the arrangement may change, so it keeps evaluating both URLs instead of consolidating cleanly, and every cold homepage visit pays an extra round trip before the first byte of content. Small in absolute terms, but it applies to the single highest-authority URL on the domain.
findings.recommendation: Serve the landing content at / instead of redirecting to it. In middleware.ts:284-289, replace NextResponse.redirect with NextResponse.rewrite(new URL(ROUTES.LANDING, request.url)) for the anonymous root case, so / returns 200 with the landing HTML; the signed-in branch keeps redirecting to /dashboard. Then set the landing canonical to "/" in app/landing/page.tsx:29 and change the sitemap entry at lib/seo/routes.ts:26 from "/landing" to "/", and 301 /landing to / so the old URL consolidates. If the redirect is kept instead, at minimum change it to a 308 (`NextResponse.redirect(url, 308)`) so it is declared permanent, and change the root layout fallback at app/layout.tsx:59 to "/landing" so it names a URL that actually renders.

findings.title: GraphQL is a single introspection probe, not a target: spec import handles OpenAPI, Swagger and Postman only, and silently drops every templated path
findings.category: list (a) gap rank 12: API scanning depth
findings.description: lib/scanner/spec-import.ts:13 declares `SpecFormat = "openapi3" | "swagger2" | "postman" | "unknown"`, and the extractor deliberately discards any path or server URL containing a `{placeholder}` (:39 to :42, :48 to :51) and caps the result at 50 targets (:21). GraphQL appears only as one of the nine active probes, "sends an introspection query to common GraphQL endpoints and flags any that return the full schema" (lib/scanner/active-probe-catalog.ts:78 to :82). Among peers, Burp Suite DAST supports Postman Collections, OpenAPI, SOAP and GraphQL with Basic, Bearer, API key and OAuth 2.0 client credentials; Snyk treats GraphQL as a first-class target including schema fetch from an introspection endpoint and claims 115 API-specific vulnerability types; Astra covers REST, SOAP and GraphQL and flags shadow and zombie APIs (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors-commercial.md).
findings.impact: For an API-first team the practical effect is that importing a spec covers only the handful of concrete paths, since a realistic REST spec is mostly `/users/{id}`-shaped, and a GraphQL service gets one yes/no answer about introspection and nothing else. Bounded, because that team is not this product's core user today, but it is the reason an API-first prospect bounces.
findings.recommendation: The cheap half is worth doing: in lib/scanner/spec-import.ts, instead of discarding a templated path, substitute a benign placeholder from the spec's own declared example or default value for that parameter, and only discard when no example exists. That alone turns a typical OpenAPI import from a handful of targets into most of the surface. The GraphQL half is genuinely medium-to-large (introspect the schema, then generate queries per type) and should wait until the introspection probe shows real usage; if it is built, reuse lib/scanner/checks/api.ts's existing category rather than adding a taxonomy value.

findings.title: There is no customer SSO or SAML: the only OIDC path is staff-only and by design never creates or promotes an account
findings.description: app/api/v3/auth/staff-oidc/route.ts:1 to :4 states the posture: the OIDC flow "never creates or promotes an account; only signs into an existing staff-or-above account whose email matches the IdP's". Customer sign-in is password plus 2FA plus Google, GitHub and Discord OAuth (app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/route.ts). A grep for saml or SAML across lib/ and app/ returns nothing. Among peers, Burp Suite DAST supports SAML, Okta and Entra ID, and Intruder lists Okta SSO; the rest are not documented to.
findings.impact: SSO is the gate on selling to a company rather than a person. With paid tiers at $5 to $20 a month and roughly 50 registered users, no prospect in that band is blocked by its absence today, and the buyers who require SAML are buying at Burp and Snyk price points with procurement processes this product is not set up for.
findings.recommendation: Do not build this now. Record it as a deliberate deferral so it stops resurfacing in feature lists. If a team plan is ever priced above roughly $200/month, the cheapest correct path is to extend the existing lib/auth/staff-oidc.ts discovery-document machinery to a per-team issuer configuration rather than adding a SAML stack, since generic OIDC covers Okta, Entra ID and Google Workspace and reuses code that is already written and audited.

findings.title: The compliance crosswalk has no evidence-push to Drata or Vanta and no PCI ASV attestation, and only the first of those is worth ever building
findings.description: lib/reports/compliance-mappings.ts:43 exposes six frameworks (pci, soc2, iso27001, asvs, hipaa, gdpr) and compliance-report.ts renders the crosswalk, but the output is a document a human downloads; nothing pushes it anywhere. Intruder offers one-click evidence push to Drata and Vanta and covers SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA and DORA. On attestation, the market is thin and expensive: Detectify resells a PCI ASV Attestation of Scan Compliance at EUR 500/yr but is not itself the ASV (it partners with Clone Systems), Intruder explicitly states it is not an ASV even though its underlying Tenable engine is, and nobody else in the eight issues one. Astra is the exception on the artifact side, issuing a publicly verifiable pentest certificate gated on passing reverification and valid 180 days (audits/AUDIT-014/research-competitors-commercial.md, "Attestation artifacts").
findings.impact: Bounded. The GRC buyer who needs a Drata evidence connector is not shopping at $20/month. The real cost of the gap is that the crosswalk currently ends at a download, so the work it represents leaves no trace in the compliance tool where the auditor actually looks.
findings.recommendation: Never pursue PCI ASV: it requires becoming an approved scanning vendor, which is a certification programme, not a feature, and Detectify's own answer was to resell someone else's. Drata and Vanta connectors are also premature. The version of this worth building is Astra's and ImmuniWeb's, and it is mostly built: a public, dated, shareable attestation page derived from the existing public host report (app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx) and the badge token machinery (app/api/v3/badge/site/route.ts), gated on the site grade from comp-03 and on a rescan proving the earlier findings gone, which lib/scanner/regression-alert.ts and lib/scanner/finding-diff.ts already compute. That is the compliance artifact a small team can actually use, and it feeds the badge loop instead of a third-party GRC vendor's.

findings.title: Negative result: the theme system, motion policy, focus policy and copy discipline are genuinely sound, and the auth flow and the scan result view are the internal reference examples to copy
findings.description: Recorded so a future audit does not redo this. (a) Theming is real, not aspirational: across all of app/ and components/ there are exactly three `dark:` class overrides (components/landing/landing-hero.tsx, components/profile/tabs/developer/schedules-section.tsx, and the shadow on the hero readout). Everything else switches via the CSS variables, which is why dsn-01's contrast fix can be made in one place. (b) Motion: app/globals.css:141-152 sets a global prefers-reduced-motion block that caps animation-duration and iteration-count, so tell-tale 14 passes product-wide even where a component uses animate-pulse. (c) Focus: app/globals.css:370-372 sets a global :focus-visible ring with a documented exclusion for Radix collection items, so tell-tale 13's focus half holds even on the elements that do not opt in locally. (d) Copy: the only em dashes in app/ and components/ are inside code comments and one empty-cell placeholder at components/admin/features/content-manager.tsx:451, so the CLAUDE.md ban is genuinely honoured; "Everything you need" survives only as mid-sentence prose at app/docs/architecture/page.tsx:77 (already AUDIT-011#design F2). (e) The auth flow is the strongest in-app work and should be the model: components/auth/auth-split-layout.tsx:77-146 is a one-canvas asymmetric layout with a real ResponseReadout, a hard-broken two-line headline and a border-l definition list, and components/auth/auth-shell.tsx:22-90 centralises the field class, focus ring, step indicator and heading so every screen in the flow is identical by construction. (f) The scan result view is the strongest data surface: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx is a genuine single source of truth, SeverityDistribution at :129-190 is one bar with a legend rather than five stat cards exactly as its docblock claims, and components/scanner/scan-summary.tsx carries zero raw palette colours across 300-odd lines. (g) The joined stat strip idiom (`grid grid-cols-2 sm:grid-cols-4 gap-px bg-border`) is the correct anti-pattern-avoidant shape and is used consistently on /dashboard, /history, /assets and /shares; only its implementation is duplicated (dsn-06), not its design.
findings.impact: None. This is a record of what was checked and found correct.
findings.recommendation: No action. When building a new in-app flow, copy components/auth/auth-shell.tsx's shape: put the shared field class, focus ring and heading component in one module per flow so the screens cannot drift. When building a new data panel, copy components/scanner/scan-summary.tsx. Point new contributors at those two files rather than at the landing page, which is a marketing surface and does not answer in-app questions.

findings.title: Verified clean: the docs surface, the email layout, and the Markdown and SARIF severity vocabulary are all consistent systems, and the AUDIT-013 label inconsistency does not reach any export
findings.description: Recording what was checked and found correct, so the next audit does not repeat it. (1) DOCS ARE ONE SYSTEM. All 19 docs pages plus app/docs/page.tsx use DocsHero and DocsSection; the chrome (breadcrumb, prev/next pager, table of contents, sidebar, mobile nav) lives once in components/docs/docs-shell.tsx:60-90 and is applied by app/docs/layout.tsx to every page, so no page can forget it. Hand-rolled cards outside the primitives total 7 across 12,000 lines of docs pages (2 in api, 3 in setup, 1 each in developers and rate-limits) and there are zero hand-rolled `<table>` elements. DocsCallout (components/docs/docs-callout.tsx:12-18) draws its four variants from semantic tokens with a left rule and an explicit docblock rejecting the icon-in-a-rounded-square. The open docs issues remain AUDIT-011#docs-03 (124-character measure), #docs-04 (shell wider than its nav), #docs-07 (unlabelled playground inputs) and #docs-11 (tablist without tabpanel); nothing new was found. (2) EMAIL HAS THE SHARED LAYOUT IT NEEDS. lib/email/email.ts:107-180 is a single layout() used by every template through sendEmail:431, with seven composition helpers (:193-332), an escapeHtml applied at every interpolation, a plain-text alternative on every template (47 `text:` keys against 46 `html:`), zero emoji, zero em dashes in user-facing strings, a 600px table with a max-width:600px media query and mobile padding overrides (:138-141), `color-scheme` and `supported-color-schemes` meta (:133-134) which is the correct guard against forced dark-mode inversion, and colours sourced from lib/config/brand.ts rather than hardcoded (:19-46). Copy voice follows the rules: mechanism-first, specific, no platitudes. The open items are dsnx-05, dsnx-06 and dsnx-11 only. (3) SEVERITY VOCABULARY IN EXPORTS IS CONSISTENT. AUDIT-013#dup-02 found `/checks` labelling info as "Informational" (lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:30) against "Info" elsewhere. That inconsistency does NOT reach any export: markdown-report.ts:31-37 and compliance-report.ts:29-34 both use "Info", pdf-report.ts:273 prints `sev.toUpperCase()`, sarif-report.ts maps to SARIF's own three levels, and CSV uses `f.severity.toUpperCase()`. Ordering is critical-to-info in all five, and findings arrive pre-sorted from lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:711. "Informational" appears in only three places repo-wide and none of them is an export. (4) THE EXTENSION POPUP DOES MATCH ITS STORE ART. store_1.png's product panel shows a risk score with a label, a severity chip row, findings with coloured left rails, and a footer with a finding count and a "Full report" link; extension/src/popup/popup.ts:331-430 renders exactly that structure, including the 3px severity rail at :508. The store screenshots are honest about the shipped UI. (5) NO HTML REPORT RENDERER EXISTS. The export set is JSON, CSV, PDF, SARIF, Markdown and the compliance crosswalk; the shared scan page at /shared/[token] is the de facto HTML report and belongs to the in-app review.
findings.impact: None. This is a record of coverage. It matters mainly for the two surfaces auditors most expect to be broken and which are not: the email system already has the shared layout that usually needs to be proposed, and the docs already read as one manual rather than twenty pages.
findings.recommendation: No action. When re-auditing section 5, start from the report renderers and the extension, which is where the real drift is, and treat lib/email/email.ts and components/docs/ as reference implementations of what a shared abstraction should look like on the other surfaces.

findings.title: Verified correct on the scanning page, recorded so the next audit does not re-derive it
findings.description:
Things I checked on this surface and found sound, so they need no work.

1. The progress denominator is genuinely real, not estimated. app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:332-339 derives `categoriesTotal` from `getPlannedSyncCategories` plus `getPlannedAsyncBranches` against the actual selected scanners, and explicitly zeroes the sync side for raw-IP targets to match executeScan's own gating. lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:117-139 persists only events the engine actually emits. Tell-tale 8 (numbers real, not hardcoded) passes on the counter, even though the bar around it does not.

2. The component's ratchet is not a stall. `MIN_STEP_DISPLAY_MS` paces the display only; the parent's `status` flip unmounts the indicator immediately on completion regardless of where the ratchet has got to. The docblock at :46-57 says so and the code matches. No artificial minimum display time exists, confirming AUDIT-011#scan-05's own negative finding still holds.

3. Colour discipline is clean. No `bg-gray-*`, `text-slate-*`, `bg-[#hex]` or raw brand constant appears in scanning-indicator.tsx, dashboard-error-state.tsx or the scanning branch of app/dashboard/page.tsx. Severity in the error card goes through `hsl(var(--severity-medium))` and `bg-destructive` (dashboard-error-state.tsx:98, 106, 216), which is the correct encoding. Tell-tale 3 passes.

4. No em dashes in any user-facing string on this page. Every `--` in these files is inside a code comment.

5. Focus rings are present on both interactive controls: the cancel button (scanning-indicator.tsx:352) and the copy button plus support link in the error card (dashboard-error-state.tsx:241, 294) all carry `focus-visible:outline-hidden focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring`. No `onClick` on a bare div anywhere on this surface. Tell-tale 13 passes on focus, fails only on semantics (scanui-08).

6. `app/dashboard/` has both `loading.tsx` and `error.tsx`, so it is not part of AUDIT-011#drift-13's missing-boundary set.

7. The per-family copy in `FAMILY_STEP` (scanning-indicator.tsx:16-36) is good, specific, mechanism-first writing that matches the voice rules: "Grepping responses for keys and tokens", "Negotiating TLS versions and ciphers", "Looking for leaked paths, versions and stack traces". The rebuild should keep these strings; the problem is the container, not the words. The only nit is the two ampersands at :35.
findings.impact: None. Recorded so a future audit of this surface starts from the open items rather than re-deriving the settled ones.
findings.recommendation: No action. When scanui-03 is built, carry points 3, 4, 5 and 7 forward rather than rewriting them.

findings.title: Negative results: pipeline secrets handling is clean, every action is SHA-pinned, and the release artifact chain works end to end
findings.description: Verified so the next audit does not repeat it. (1) No workflow uses `pull_request_target`, `secrets: inherit`, or `workflow_call`; grep across .github/ returns nothing for all three. (2) The only secret referenced anywhere in .github/ is `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (7 references across 5 files); no third-party credential is present in the pipeline. (3) No secret is passed as a Docker build arg or baked into an image ENV: Dockerfile:16 declares only `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` as an ARG and lines 37-40 set placeholder values, with the comment at 41-44 explaining that API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is deliberately left unset so it fails closed. (4) No untrusted `github.event.*` field is interpolated into a `run:` body; release.yml routes `release.tag_name` and `workflow_run.head_branch` through `env:` at lines 86-88 with a comment naming the CodeQL rule, and docker-publish.yml:40 and 43 use the `GITHUB_REF_NAME` and `GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER` shell variables rather than expressions. (5) All 23 `uses:` lines across the seven workflows are pinned to a 40-character commit SHA with a version comment (23 of 23 match `@[0-9a-f]{40}`). (6) Permissions are scoped per workflow or per job everywhere except label.yml (see ci-05); ci.yml is `contents: read`, docker-publish.yml scopes `packages: write` and `id-token: write` to the one job that needs them, release.yml scopes `contents: write` and `id-token: write` to its one job. (7) `continue-on-error` appears exactly once (release.yml:168, see ci-12) and there is no `|| true` anywhere. (8) `npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev` currently reports 0 vulnerabilities, so the gate at ci.yml:71 is passing rather than being routed around. (9) next.config.mjs sets no `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors`; `eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds: true` at line 23 is compensated by the standalone `npm run lint` step at ci.yml:40. `output: "standalone"` is deliberately absent and consistent with Dockerfile:75-79 copying `.next` and `node_modules` (line 4-8 comment). (10) The CI knowledge-drift gate works: I confirmed empirically that `git diff --exit-code --ignore-matching-lines='compiled from'` ignores a date-only change and still exits 1 on a real content change, and the date lines in all five generated files contain the string "compiled from". (11) The release artifact chain is live and correct: I fetched the releases API and v3.6.0 through v3.7.2 each carry the tarball, the `.tar.gz.cert` cosign bundle, `sha256sums.txt`, both extension zips, and the CycloneDX SBOM, and the asset names match exactly what lib/updater/apply.ts:85-88 looks for. (12) Nothing can publish an image from a branch push: docker-publish.yml triggers only on `push: tags: v*`.

findings.title: Negative results for the next audit: root .env.local is correctly excluded from the image, the container runs non-root with a real healthcheck and shutdown handlers, and Stripe, AI, Turnstile and Browserbase all degrade gracefully when unset
findings.description: Recorded so the next audit does not re-derive them. All static, nothing executed. (1) Secret leak into the image: root .env.local IS matched by both `.env.*` and `.env*.local` at .dockerignore:5-6 and never enters the context; `!.env.example` at :7 correctly re-includes only the template. The nested caveat is host-11. (2) The `*.md` exclusion at .dockerignore:9 is root-anchored and therefore does not strip the five generated AI knowledge files under lib/ai/, and the prebuild compilers (package.json:13) read .ts sources (scripts/compile-changelog-knowledge.mjs:26 reads lib/changelog/data.ts), so the build is not broken by it. (3) Non-root: Dockerfile:71-72 creates uid/gid 1001 and :102 switches to it before EXPOSE. (4) HEALTHCHECK at Dockerfile:99-100 and docker-compose.yml:87-99 both target /api/v3/health, which does a real pool.connect plus a schema-version and required-tables probe (app/api/v3/health/route.ts:88-116) rather than the GitHub-only /api/version, and the path is in lib/config/public-paths.ts:109 so middleware does not block the probe. (5) Compose ordering is correct: the app depends_on postgres with condition: service_healthy (docker-compose.yml:79-81) against a pg_isready healthcheck (:26-30), so there is no startup race. postgres_data (:115) persists across `docker compose down`, and app/docs/setup/page.tsx:679-680 correctly flags `down -v` as the destructive variant. (6) Postgres 16.4-alpine (:18) satisfies the documented 14+ floor in README.md:124. (7) Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers close the pool at the end of instrumentation.ts's register(), and tini is PID 1 (Dockerfile:114). (8) Optional integrations fail soft, not hard: Turnstile is gated behind TURNSTILE_ENABLED at app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:41 so signup works with no keys; the AI provider, Stripe and Browserbase are all optional in the lib/config/env.ts OptionalSchema and none is read at boot. (9) There is no seeded account and no default password anywhere in the fresh-install path: scripts/create-fresh-db/create-fresh-db.mjs seeds only default badges, and the first admin is made by hand via SQL per app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:276-284.
findings.impact: None. This records the parts of the self-host surface that are correct so a future audit can spend its time on host-01 through host-08 instead.
